## Statement

For every nonstationary trial of [[alg-trust-region-method]], the selected
predicted reduction is positive, and every accepted trial strictly decreases
the objective.

Assume the hypotheses and parameter ranges of
[[thm-trust-region-global-liminf-gradient]], and let $f_{inf}$ be a lower
bound for $f$. For each target $0<\varepsilon\le1$, run
[[alg-trust-region-method]] until its first iterate with
$\|\nabla f(x_k)\|_2\le\varepsilon$. Define
$$c_\delta:=\min\left\{\frac1{2M_B},
\frac{\theta_C(1-\eta_2)}{2(L+M_B)}\right\},\qquad
c_R:=\min\{\Delta_0,\gamma_{dec}\min\{c_\delta,\Delta_{max}\}\},$$
where a zero denominator means $+\infty$, and put
$$c_P:=\min\{c_R,1/M_B\},\qquad
c_S:=\tfrac12\eta_1\theta_Cc_P>0.$$
Then the number $N_s$ of accepted steps before reaching the target and the
number $N_u$ of rejected trials obey
$$N_s\le\frac{f(x_0)-f_{inf}}{c_S\varepsilon^2},$$
$$N_u\le\frac{\log(\Delta_0/r_\varepsilon)+N_s\log\gamma_{inc}}
{|\log\gamma_{dec}|},\qquad
r_\varepsilon:=\min\{\Delta_0,\gamma_{dec}\min\{c_\delta\varepsilon,
\Delta_{max}\}\}.$$
Here $\log$ denotes the natural logarithm of a positive real.
Consequently, accepted steps and total trials $N_s+N_u$ are
$O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. An outer cap at least
the resulting total-trial bound suffices for the finite-budget algorithm to
return `target-achieved` or `stationary`, with gradient norm at most
$\varepsilon$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The model-Hessian bound, gradient Lipschitz bound, bounded-below
objective, parameter ranges, and step safeguard of the trust-region method.

[F1] [[alg-trust-region-method]]: each step has predicted reduction at least
$\theta_C$ times the Cauchy decrease; a rejection multiplies $\Delta$ by
$\gamma_{dec}$; an accepted update multiplies it by a factor in
$[1,\gamma_{inc}]$, respecting $\Delta_{max}$.

[F2] [[lem-trust-region-cauchy-decrease]]: if $a:=\|g_k\|_2>0$, then
$$m_k(0)-m_k(p_C)\ge\tfrac12a\min\{\Delta_k,a/\|B_k\|_2\},$$
with the zero-matrix convention stated there.

[F3] [[lem-trust-region-ratio-accuracy-for-small-radii]]: when
$a\ge\varepsilon$ and $\Delta_k\le c_\delta\varepsilon$, the algorithm's
small-radius branch gives $\rho_k\ge\eta_2$ and uses the boundary Cauchy
step, so rejection is impossible.

[F4] [[def-natural-logarithm]]: $\log x$ is defined for $x>0$ as the inverse
of the real exponential.

[F5] [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: $\log$ is strictly increasing,
$\log1=0$, and the product and quotient laws hold for positive arguments.

[F6] [[lem-natural-logarithm-bounded-by-argument]]:
$0\le\log y\le y-1\le y$ for $y\ge1$.

[F7] [[thm-of-archimedean]]: for every real $R$ there is an integer
$m\in\mathbb N$ with $m>R$.

[F8] [[lem-geometric-sequence-null]]: if $0<q<1$, then $q^j\to0$ as
$j\to\infty$.

[A1] The target satisfies $0<\varepsilon\le1$.

[A2] Every model matrix is symmetric with norm at most $M_B$, and the
gradient is $L$-Lipschitz on every trial segment.

[A3] The objective satisfies $f(x)\ge f_{inf}$ at all iterates.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Let $\bar\delta_\varepsilon:=
\min\{c_\delta\varepsilon,\Delta_{max}\}$. Every radius during a
pre-target trial is at least
$$r_\varepsilon=\min\{\Delta_0,\gamma_{dec}\bar\delta_\varepsilon\}>0.$$
Indeed, this holds initially. If a trial is rejected, [F3] implies its
radius exceeded $\bar\delta_\varepsilon$, since at or below that threshold
the ratio is at least $\eta_2$; after multiplication by $\gamma_{dec}$ the
new radius is greater than $\gamma_{dec}\bar\delta_\varepsilon$. An
accepted update does not decrease the radius. Induction proves the bound.
[given, A1, A2, F1, F3, induction, algebra]

1.2 If the target were never reached, every rejection block would be finite:
an infinite block would multiply a fixed radius by $\gamma_{dec}^j\to0$ by
[F8], eventually making $\Delta\le\bar\delta_\varepsilon$, where [F3]
forbids rejection. Thus an infinite pre-target run would contain infinitely
many accepted trials. For any accepted trial its starting gradient norm
$a$ exceeds $\varepsilon$. From step 1.1,
$\Delta_k\ge r_\varepsilon\ge c_R\varepsilon$, because
$\varepsilon\le1$ and
$$\min\{c_\delta\varepsilon,\Delta_{max}\}
\ge\varepsilon\min\{c_\delta,\Delta_{max}\}.$$
Since $\Delta_0\ge\varepsilon\Delta_0$, taking the minimum with
$\Delta_0$ in the definition of $r_\varepsilon$ gives
$r_\varepsilon\ge c_R\varepsilon$.
Also $a/\|B_k\|_2\ge\varepsilon/M_B$, with the stated infinity
convention if $M_B=0$. Hence
$$\min\{\Delta_k,a/\|B_k\|_2\}\ge c_P\varepsilon.$$
By [F1] and [F2], the predicted reduction is at least
$\tfrac12\theta_Cc_P\varepsilon^2$. Acceptance gives actual decrease at
least $\eta_1$ times this amount, namely $c_S\varepsilon^2$. If the target
were never reached, after $m$ accepted trials the objective would be at most
$f(x_0)-m c_S\varepsilon^2$. By [F7] choose an integer
$m>(f(x_0)-f_{inf})/(c_S\varepsilon^2)$; this contradicts [A3]. Therefore
the target is reached after finitely many accepted trials. Summing their
decreases gives
$N_s c_S\varepsilon^2\le f(x_0)-f_{inf}$, the claimed successful-step
bound. [given, A1, A2, A3, F1, F2, F3, F7, F8, step 1.1, choose,
assume-contra, discharge-contradiction, algebra]

2.1 Let $\Delta_T$ be the radius after the accepted trial that first
reaches the target. Each rejected trial multiplies the radius by
$\gamma_{dec}$; each accepted update multiplies it by some
$r_j\in[1,\gamma_{inc}]$. Therefore
$$\Delta_T=\Delta_0\gamma_{dec}^{N_u}\prod_{j=1}^{N_s}r_j.$$
Step 1.1 gives $\Delta_T\ge r_\varepsilon$. By [F5],
$\log\gamma_{dec}<0$, and logarithms of positive products give
$$\log\Delta_T=\log\Delta_0+N_u\log\gamma_{dec}
+\sum_{j=1}^{N_s}\log r_j.$$
Rearranging and using $\log r_j\le\log\gamma_{inc}$ yields
$$N_u|\log\gamma_{dec}|
=\log(\Delta_0/\Delta_T)+\sum_{j=1}^{N_s}\log r_j
\le\log(\Delta_0/r_\varepsilon)+N_s\log\gamma_{inc},$$
which proves the rejection bound, including every rejected trial.
[given, F1, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Since $r_\varepsilon\ge c_R\varepsilon$ for
$0<\varepsilon\le1$, [F5] gives
$$\log(\Delta_0/r_\varepsilon)
\le\log(\Delta_0/(c_R\varepsilon))
=\log(\Delta_0/c_R)+\log(1/\varepsilon).$$
By [F6], $\log(1/\varepsilon)\le1/\varepsilon$; since
$0<\varepsilon\le1$, $1/\varepsilon\le1/\varepsilon^2$. Thus the radius
term is $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$, as is $N_s$ by step 1.2, so
$N_s+N_u=O(\varepsilon^{-2})$. If the finite outer cap
allows at least that many trials, the process reaches the target before the
cap. [given, F5, F6, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.1 For any nonstationary trial, $\|g_k\|_2>0$ and $\Delta_k>0$.
By [F2], the Cauchy step has $P_C>0$. The selection rule either chooses a
candidate with predicted decrease at least $\theta_C P_C$, or uses $p_C$;
the small-radius override also uses $p_C$. Since $0<\theta_C\le1$, every
branch therefore gives $P_k\ge\theta_C P_C>0$, so the ratio in the
algorithm is defined. [F1, F2, given, cases, algebra]

4.1 On an accepted trial, $\rho_k\ge\eta_1>0$ and $P_k>0$ by step 3.1.
Thus $f(x_{k+1})=f(x_k)-\rho_kP_k<f(x_k)$, proving strict decrease at every
accepted trial. [F1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$, bounded below, and have an
$L$-Lipschitz gradient on every trial segment. At every iteration let $B_k$
be symmetric with $\|B_k\|_2\le M_B$ for a fixed $M_B\ge0$. Run an infinite
trust-region process of [[alg-trust-region-method]] with no positive target
and no outer cap, fixed $0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1$,
$0<\gamma_{dec}<1<\gamma_{inc}$, $0<\theta_C\le1$, and
$0<\Delta_0\le\Delta_{max}$. If it does not terminate at a stationary
point, then
$$\liminf_{k\to\infty}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|_2=0.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The smoothness, boundedness, and update assumptions of the
Statement and the algorithm's Cauchy-decrease safeguard.

[F1] [[alg-trust-region-method]]: every selected step has predicted
reduction at least $\theta_C$ times the Cauchy decrease; when
$\Delta_k\le\|g_k\|_2/(2M_B)$, the algorithm uses the Cauchy step. A rejected
trial multiplies the radius by $\gamma_{dec}$; an accepted trial either
keeps it or increases it, capped by $\Delta_{max}$.

[F2] [[lem-trust-region-cauchy-decrease]]: for $g_k\ne0$,
$$m_k(0)-m_k(p_C)\ge\tfrac12\|g_k\|_2
\min\{\Delta_k,\|g_k\|_2/\|B_k\|_2\},$$
with the zero-matrix convention stated there.

[F3] [[lem-trust-region-ratio-accuracy-for-small-radii]]: if
$\|g_k\|_2\ge\varepsilon>0$ and
$$\Delta_k\le\min\left\{\frac{\varepsilon}{2M_B},
\frac{\theta_C(1-\eta_2)\varepsilon}{2(L+M_B)}\right\},$$
then $\rho_k\ge\eta_2$ for a step with the stated Cauchy-decrease fraction.
Zero denominators mean $+\infty$.

[F4] [[lem-geometric-sequence-null]]: if $0<q<1$, then $q^j\to0$ as
$j\to\infty$.

[F5] [[def-limsup-liminf]]: $\liminf_k a_k=\sup_n i_n$, where
$i_n:=\inf\{a_k:k\ge n\}$.

[F6] [[lem-extended-reals-complete]]: every tail has a greatest lower bound
in $\overline{\mathbb R}$; it lies below every tail element and above every
other lower bound.

[F7] [[def-upper-bound]]: if every element of a set is at most $b$, then $b$
is an upper bound and its supremum is at most $b$.

[A1] $f$ has a finite lower bound on $\mathbb R^n$.

[A2] Every $B_k$ is symmetric and obeys $\|B_k\|_2\le M_B$.

[A3] $\nabla f$ is $L$-Lipschitz on each generated trial segment.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Fix any $\varepsilon>0$ and suppose that $\|g_k\|_2\ge\varepsilon$
for every $k\ge K$. Put
$$d_\varepsilon:=\min\left\{\frac{\varepsilon}{2M_B},
\frac{\theta_C(1-\eta_2)\varepsilon}{2(L+M_B)}\right\},\qquad
\bar d_\varepsilon:=\min\{d_\varepsilon,\Delta_{max}\},$$

## Statement

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then:

1. If $(X,d_X)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]), the image
   $f[X] \subseteq Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$.
2. More generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$, then $f[K]$ is
   a compact subset of $Y$.

No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Metric spaces $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ and a continuous $f : X \to Y$; images and preimages are written $f[\,\cdot\,]$ and $f^{-1}[\,\cdot\,]$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

[L1] A subset $A$ of a metric space is compact exactly when for every family $(V_i)_{i \in I}$ of open subsets of the ambient space with $A \subseteq \bigcup_{i \in I} V_i$ there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $i_0, \dots, i_n \in I$ with $A \subseteq V_{i_0} \cup \dots \cup V_{i_n}$, or else $A = \emptyset$; and a space is a compact subset of itself exactly when it is a compact metric space ([[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]], [[def-metric-compactness]]).

[L2] $f$ is continuous exactly when $f^{-1}[V]$ is open in $X$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$ ([[thm-metric-continuity-characterisations]], [[def-metric-continuity]], [[def-metric-topology]]).

[L3] The restriction of $f$ to a metric subspace $(K,d_K)$ of $X$ is continuous as a map $(K,d_K) \to (Y,d_Y)$, since the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition at a point of $K$ is the condition for $f$ at that point read for the points of $K$ only, and $d_K$ is the restriction of $d_X$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]], [[def-metric-continuity]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Assume $(X,d_X)$ compact and let $(V_i)_{i \in I}$ be a family of open subsets of $Y$ with $f[X] \subseteq \bigcup_{i \in I} V_i$. [L1]

2.1 Each $f^{-1}[V_i]$ is open in $X$, and $X = \bigcup_{i \in I} f^{-1}[V_i]$, because every $x \in X$ has $f(x) \in f[X]$ and so $f(x) \in V_i$ for some $i$. [L2, step 1.1]

3.1 If $X = \emptyset$ then $f[X] = \emptyset$ and there is nothing to prove; otherwise compactness of $X$, read against the indexed family of step 2.1, gives $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $i_0, \dots, i_n \in I$ with $X = f^{-1}[V_{i_0}] \cup \dots \cup f^{-1}[V_{i_n}]$. [L1, step 2.1]

4.1 Every $y \in f[X]$ is $f(x)$ for some $x \in X$, and that $x$ lies in some $f^{-1}[V_{i_j}]$, so $y \in V_{i_j}$; hence $f[X] \subseteq V_{i_0} \cup \dots \cup V_{i_n}$ and $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$: claim 1. [L1, step 3.1]

5.1 For claim 2, let $K \subseteq X$ be a compact subset, so that $(K,d_K)$ is a compact metric space; the restriction of $f$ to $K$ is continuous, and its image is $f[K]$, so claim 1 applied to that restriction gives that $f[K]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. [L1, L3, step 4.1] ∎

## Remarks

**Compactness travels forwards, not backwards.** The preimage of a compact set under a continuous map need not be compact: a constant map from an unbounded space has a one-point image. What claim 1 uses is that preimages of *open* sets are open, which is the content of continuity, together with the fact that a finite subcover upstairs projects to a finite subcover downstairs.

**Consequences on this page.** Claim 1 with $Y = \mathbb{R}$ gives the extreme value theorem ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]), and claim 2 is what makes the inverse of a continuous bijection from a compact space continuous ([[thm-continuous-bijection-from-a-compact-space-has-continuous-inverse]]).

## Statement

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $K \subseteq X$ be a
compact subset ([[def-metric-compactness]]). Then $K$ is closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

No choice principle is used: both covers below are given by a rule, and the
indexed form of [[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]] returns indices rather than
sets.

**The converse is false in general.** A closed and bounded subset of an arbitrary
metric space need not be compact
([[fs-closed-and-bounded-implies-compact-in-every-metric-space]]); it is exactly
in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that the converse holds ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A metric space $(X,d)$ and a compact subset $K \subseteq X$.

[L1] $K$ is a compact subset exactly when for every set $I$ and every family $(U_i)_{i \in I}$ of open subsets of $X$ with $K \subseteq \bigcup_{i \in I} U_i$ there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $i_0, \dots, i_n \in I$ with $K \subseteq U_{i_0} \cup \dots \cup U_{i_n}$, or else $K = \emptyset$ ([[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]], [[def-metric-compactness]]).

[L2] For $p \ne x$ in $X$ and $r := d(p,x)/2$ one has $r > 0$ and $B(p,r) \cap B(x,r) = \emptyset$ ([[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]).

[L3] Open balls are open, $X$ is open, and a set is closed exactly when its complement is open ([[thm-metric-open-set-algebra]], [[def-metric-topology]], [[def-metric-ball]]).

[L4] A nonempty finite set of reals has a maximum and a minimum, each one of its members ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

[L5] A subset is bounded when it is empty or contained in some ball $B(x_0,r)$ with $r > 0$; and $B(x_0,s) \subseteq B(x_0,r)$ whenever $0 < s \le r$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[def-metric-ball]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $K = \emptyset$ then $K$ is bounded by the first clause of the definition, and it is closed because $X \setminus K = X$ is open. [L3, L5]

1.2 Assume from now on that $K \ne \emptyset$ and fix $p \in K$; the family $(B(p,r))_{r \in P}$ indexed by the set $P$ of positive reals consists of open sets and covers $K$, since every $x \in K$ satisfies $d(p,x) < d(p,x) + 1$ and so lies in $B(p, d(p,x)+1)$. [L3, L5]

2.1 The indexed characterisation gives $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and positive reals $r_0, \dots, r_n$ with $K \subseteq B(p,r_0) \cup \dots \cup B(p,r_n)$; putting $R := \max\{r_0, \dots, r_n\}$, a positive real, the balls with common centre $p$ are nested, so $K \subseteq B(p,R)$ and $K$ is bounded. [L1, L4, L5, step 1.2]

3.1 Boundedness being settled, take up closedness: let $q \in X \setminus K$ and for each $x \in K$ put $r_x := d(q,x)/2$, which is a positive real because $q \ne x$, and which satisfies $B(q,r_x) \cap B(x,r_x) = \emptyset$. [L2, step 2.1]

4.1 The family $(B(x,r_x))_{x \in K}$ consists of open subsets of $X$ and covers $K$, since $x \in B(x,r_x)$; so there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $x_0, \dots, x_n \in K$ with $K \subseteq B(x_0, r_{x_0}) \cup \dots \cup B(x_n, r_{x_n})$. [L1, L3, step 3.1]

5.1 Put $r := \min\{r_{x_0}, \dots, r_{x_n}\}$, a positive real. [L4, step 4.1]

6.1 Then $B(q,r) \cap K = \emptyset$: a point $y$ of the intersection would lie in $B(x_i, r_{x_i})$ for some $i \le n$ by step 4.1, and also in $B(q,r) \subseteq B(q, r_{x_i})$ by step 5.1, whereas those two balls are disjoint by step 3.1. [L5, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1]

7.1 So every point of $X \setminus K$ has a ball around it inside $X \setminus K$, that set is open, and $K$ is closed; together with steps 1.1 and 2.1 this proves the theorem. [L3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 6.1] ∎

## Remarks

**Both conclusions use compactness through the same characterisation.** The first cover is by concentric balls of every positive radius, which is what boundedness is about; the second is by balls small enough to keep a fixed outside point away, which is what closedness is about. In each case what compactness returns is a finite list of indices, and a maximum or a minimum of finitely many positive reals then does the rest.

**Hausdorffness is what makes the second argument work**, and every metric space has it ([[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]). The statement is false for topological spaces without that separation property, which is why the proof cites the separation lemma rather than the metric axioms directly.

## Statement

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below. Then $S$ has a
greatest lower bound in $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-infimum]]), and it is given by

$$\inf S = -\sup(-S), \qquad \text{where } -S = \{-s : s \in S\}.$$

In particular the complete ordered field $\mathbb{R}$ has the
greatest-lower-bound property, which is therefore not an extra axiom: it is a
consequence of the least-upper-bound property.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonempty $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ that is bounded below, and its reflection $-S = \{-s : s \in S\}$.

[L1] The least-upper-bound property of $\mathbb{R}$: every nonempty subset of $\mathbb{R}$ that is bounded above has a least upper bound in $\mathbb{R}$, namely an upper bound that is $\le$ every upper bound ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

[L2] Reflection: $-(-S) = S$; $S$ is nonempty exactly when $-S$ is; $u$ is an upper bound of a set $X$ exactly when $-u$ is a lower bound of $-X$; and $\ell$ is a lower bound of $X$ exactly when $-\ell$ is an upper bound of $-X$ ([[lem-reflection]]).

[L3] Greatest lower bound (infimum): $\ell$ is one for $S$ when $\ell$ is a lower bound of $S$ and $\ell' \le \ell$ for every lower bound $\ell'$ of $S$ ([[def-infimum]]).

[L4] A least upper bound and a greatest lower bound are unique when they exist, so the notations $\sup$ and $\inf$ are unambiguous ([[lem-sup-unique]]).

[L5] Negation reverses the order, elementwise: $-(-a) = a$, because $(-a) + a = 0$ and additive inverses are unique ([[def-field]], [[lem-of-inverse-unique]]); and $a \le b$ if and only if $-b \le -a$, because translation invariance applied with the constant $-a - b$ turns $a < b$ into $-b < -a$ and, applied with the constant $a + b$, turns $-b < -a$ back into $a < b$, while $a = b$ holds exactly when $-a = -b$ ([[lem-of-add-order]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By hypothesis $S \ne \emptyset$ and $S$ is bounded below; fix a lower bound $\ell_0$ of $S$, so $\ell_0 \le s$ for every $s \in S$. [given, choose]

1.2 Let $\ell'$ be an arbitrary lower bound of $S$; then $-\ell'$ is an upper bound of $-S$. [assume-hyp, L2]

2.1 Since $S$ is nonempty, so is $-S$, and since $\ell_0$ is a lower bound of $S$, its negative $-\ell_0$ is an upper bound of $-S$; hence $-S$ is a nonempty subset of $\mathbb{R}$ that is bounded above. [step 1.1, L2]

3.1 By the least-upper-bound property, $-S$ has a least upper bound in $\mathbb{R}$; write $u := \sup(-S)$, which is well defined by uniqueness. [step 2.1, L1, L4]

4.1 Define $\ell := -u$. [step 3.1, construct]

4.2 The element $u$ is the least of the upper bounds of $-S$ and $-\ell'$ is one of them, hence $u \le -\ell'$. [step 1.2, step 3.1, L1]

5.1 Apply the reflection fact to the set $-S$: since $u$ is an upper bound of $-S$, its negative $-u$ is a lower bound of $-(-S)$, and $-(-S) = S$; so $\ell = -u$ is a lower bound of $S$. [step 4.1, step 3.1, L2]

5.2 Negating the inequality $u \le -\ell'$ reverses it, giving $-(-\ell') \le -u$, that is $\ell' \le \ell$. [step 4.2, step 4.1, L5]

6.1 Thus $\ell$ is a lower bound of $S$ satisfying $\ell' \le \ell$ for every lower bound $\ell'$ of $S$, so $\ell$ is a greatest lower bound of $S$; it is the only one, so $\inf S$ exists and $\inf S = \ell = -\sup(-S)$. [step 5.1, step 5.2, L3, L4] ∎

## Remarks

- The theorem is not a restatement of the least-upper-bound property: it is proved from it, by transporting the problem across the order-reversing bijection $x \mapsto -x$ of [[lem-reflection]]. Nothing about $\mathbb{R}$ beyond the complete-ordered-field axioms is used.
- The hypotheses are both needed. The empty set is bounded below by every real and has no greatest lower bound, and a set unbounded below has no lower bound at all; the dual failures for suprema are recorded in [[fs-every-set-has-sup]].
- The identity $\inf S = -\sup(-S)$ is the standard device for turning any statement about suprema into its dual; [[lem-inf-epsilon]] is the first application on this page.

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}3&1&1/2\\1&2&1\\1/2&1&3\end{pmatrix}$$

## Definition

A **box** in $\mathbb R^n$ is $D_0=\prod_{j=1}^n[a_j,b_j]$ with finite real endpoints $a_j\le b_j$. Here $n\ge1$. The box is closed and bounded, hence compact by [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]. An **optimization instance on a compact box** consists of this $D_0$, a continuous objective $f:D_0\to\mathbb R$ (continuity in the inherited Euclidean metric, as in [[def-metric-continuity]]), and a feasible set $C\subseteq D_0$. The unconstrained instance has $C=D_0$. A constrained instance may specify $C=\{x\in D_0:g_i(x)\le0,\ 1\le i\le m\}$ for a finite list of real functions $g_i$.

When $C\ne\emptyset$, the set $f[C]$ is nonempty and bounded below: $D_0$ is compact by [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], its continuous image $f[D_0]$ is compact in the usual metric on $\mathbb R$ by [[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]] and therefore bounded by [[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]. Thus $f[D_0]$ lies in a real interval $(c-r,c+r)$ for some $c\in\mathbb R$ and $r>0$, by [[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]; hence $c-r$ is a lower bound of $f[C]\subseteq f[D_0]$. Therefore [[thm-infimum-property]] gives the real number $f^*=\inf f[C]$, using [[def-infimum]]. No attainment is assumed for a general $C$. Statements about finite empty-set detection require a separate constraint certificate or a stated separation margin; objective continuity alone does not certify infeasibility.

## Definition

A **box** in $\mathbb R^n$ is $D_0=\prod_{j=1}^n[a_j,b_j]$ with finite real endpoints $a_j\le b_j$. Here $n\ge1$. The box is closed and bounded, hence compact by [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]. An **optimization instance on a compact box** consists of this $D_0$, a continuous objective $f:D_0\to\mathbb R$ (continuity in the inherited Euclidean metric, as in [[def-metric-continuity]]), and a feasible set $C\subseteq D_0$. The unconstrained instance has $C=D_0$. A constrained instance may specify $C=\{x\in D_0:g_i(x)\le0,\ 1\le i\le m\}$ for a finite list of real functions $g_i$.

When $C\ne\emptyset$, the set $f[C]$ is nonempty and bounded below: $D_0$ is compact by [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], its continuous image $f[D_0]$ is compact in the usual metric on $\mathbb R$ by [[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]] and therefore bounded by [[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]. Thus $f[D_0]$ lies in a real interval $(c-r,c+r)$ for some $c\in\mathbb R$ and $r>0$, by [[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]; hence $c-r$ is a lower bound of $f[C]\subseteq f[D_0]$. Therefore [[thm-infimum-property]] gives the real number $f^*=\inf f[C]$, using [[def-infimum]]. No attainment is assumed for a general $C$. Statements about finite empty-set detection require a separate constraint certificate or a stated separation margin; objective continuity alone does not certify infeasibility.

    - title: "Prabhakar Poupart and Jingjing Wan, CS475/CS675 Lecture 4: Sparse Gaussian Elimination, Graph Representation, slides 6–10, University of Waterloo, May 12, 2016"
      url: "https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/~ppoupart/teaching/cs475-spring16/slides/cs475-lecture4.pdf"
dependency_level: 1

## Statement

Let $F$ be a field, let $A\in M_{n\times n}(F)$ satisfy $A_{ij}=A_{ji}$ for
all $i,j<n$, and fix an elimination ordering,
and let $G_k=(V_k,E_k)$ be its symbolic filled graphs from
[[def-symmetric-structural-elimination-graph-and-ordering]]. Put $S^0=A$.
Assume each pivot $p_k:=S^k_{v_kv_k}$ is nonzero, and for every pair of
remaining vertices define the Schur update

$$S^{k+1}_{ij}:=S^k_{ij}-\frac{S^k_{iv_k}S^k_{v_kj}}{p_k}.$$

Then for every stage $k$, each nonzero off-diagonal entry $S^k_{ij}$ has
$\{i,j\}\in E_k$. At each elimination step, the later neighbors of the
eliminated vertex form a clique in the next filled graph. Thus the symbolic
filled graph contains the numerical Schur-complement support; equality is not
asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, a symmetric matrix in $M_{n\times n}(F)$, a fixed elimination ordering, nonzero pivots, and the Schur-complement update in the Statement.

[L1] [[def-symmetric-structural-elimination-graph-and-ordering]]: at step $k$, the graph deletes $v_k$, retains edges between remaining vertices, and adds every edge between distinct vertices of $N_k(v_k)$.

[L2] [[def-field]]: division by a nonzero pivot means multiplication by its multiplicative inverse.

[L3] [[lem-of-zero-mult]]: in a field, $0\cdot a=0$ for every $a$.

[L4] [[lem-of-no-zero-divisors]]: in a field, $ab=0$ implies $a=0$ or $b=0$.

[A1] For every $k<n$, $p_k\ne0$ and $S^{k+1}_{ij}=S^k_{ij}-S^k_{iv_k}S^k_{v_kj}/p_k$ for all $i,j\in V_{k+1}$.

## Proof

1.1 At stage $0$, $S^0=A$ and the initial edge set consists exactly of the unordered off-diagonal pairs with nonzero matrix entry. Hence every nonzero off-diagonal entry of $S^0$ corresponds to an edge of $G_0$. [given, L1, algebra]

1.2 Suppose the support inclusion holds at stage $k$. If $S^{k+1}_{ij}\ne0$ for distinct $i,j\in V_{k+1}$, then at least one of $S^k_{ij}$ and $S^k_{iv_k}S^k_{v_kj}/p_k$ is nonzero. In the first case, the induction hypothesis gives $\{i,j\}\in E_k$, and the update retains that edge. In the second case, the numerator is nonzero because a zero numerator would give a zero quotient by [L2] and [L3]; then [L4] forces both pivot couplings to be nonzero. The induction hypothesis gives $\{i,v_k\},\{v_k,j\}\in E_k$, so $i,j\in N_k(v_k)$ and the update adds $\{i,j\}$. Thus every such nonzero is supported by an edge of $G_{k+1}$. [A1, L1, L2, L3, L4, induction, algebra]

2.1 The base case and induction step prove the support inclusion at every stage. For any two distinct later neighbors of $v_k$, the graph update inserts their pair by definition, so the later-neighbor set is a clique in $G_{k+1}$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L1, induction] ∎

## Remarks

The conclusion is a support inclusion, not equality: an arithmetic subtraction can cancel a nonzero entry while the symbolic edge remains. The companion page gives an explicit cancellation calculation in [[ex-numerical-cancellation-within-filled-graph]]. No factorization-cost bound follows from this graph statement.

title: "Even-power expansion of trapezoid levels with a uniform remainder"
status: draft

      locator: "Printed pp. 230–233, finite Euler–Maclaurin remainders and trapezoid expansion."
    - title: "NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, §3.5(iii), Romberg Integration"
      url: "https://dlmf.nist.gov/3.5"
      locator: "Full-text section §3.5(iii), equations 3.5.9–3.5.12 on the finite even-power expansion and Romberg recurrence."
---

## Statement

Let $a<b$, let $j\ge1$ be an integer, and let $f\in C^{2j+2}([a,b])$. For $N\ge1$ set $h=(b-a)/N$, $I=\int_a^b f$, and
$$c_r:=\frac{B_{2r}}{(2r)!}\bigl(f^{(2r-1)}(b)-f^{(2r-1)}(a)\bigr),\qquad 1\le r\le j+1,$$
using the Bernoulli numbers of [[def-na-bernoulli-polynomials]]. Then
$$T_N(f)=I+\sum_{r=1}^{j}c_rh^{2r}+\varepsilon_N,\qquad |\varepsilon_N|\le C_jh^{2j+2},$$
where the level-independent finite constant
$$C_j:=|c_{j+1}|+\frac{(b-a)M_{2j+2}}{(2j+2)!}\|f^{(2j+2)}\|_\infty,\qquad M_{2j+2}:=\max_{0\le u\le1}|B_{2j+2}(u)|,$$
does not depend on $N$. Thus the remainder bound is uniform over every set of dyadic levels.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $a<b$, an integer $j\ge1$, $f\in C^{2j+2}([a,b])$, and an integer trapezoid panel count $N\ge1$.

[F1] [[thm-na-euler-maclaurin-composite-trapezoid-remainder]]: for every $p\ge1$, the composite trapezoid equals the integral, the first $p$ endpoint Bernoulli corrections, and a remainder bounded by $(b-a)M_{2p}h^{2p}\|f^{(2p)}\|_\infty/(2p)!$.

[F2] [[def-higher-derivatives-and-smoothness]]: $C^{2j+2}$ supplies all continuous endpoint derivatives through order $2j+2$.

[F3] [[def-composite-trapezoidal-rule]]: $T_N(f)$ uses the uniform mesh of width $h=(b-a)/N$.

[F4] [[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]]: continuous real functions on the compact interval $[a,b]$ are bounded and attain finite extrema.

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F1] with $p=j+1$. The formula has the displayed coefficients $c_1,\ldots,c_{j+1}$ and a remainder $\rho_N$ satisfying $|\rho_N|\le (b-a)M_{2j+2}h^{2j+2}\|f^{(2j+2)}\|_\infty/(2j+2)!$. [given, F1, F2, F3]

2.1 By [F2] and [F4], each derivative norm in $c_{j+1}$ and $C_j$ is finite; the Bernoulli maximum exists by the Euler–Maclaurin theorem's construction. Put $\varepsilon_N:=c_{j+1}h^{2j+2}+\rho_N$. The triangle inequality gives $|\varepsilon_N|\le\bigl(|c_{j+1}|+(b-a)M_{2j+2}\|f^{(2j+2)}\|_\infty/(2j+2)!\bigr)h^{2j+2}=C_jh^{2j+2}$. Every term in $C_j$ depends only on $f,a,b,j$, not on $N$, so this is the claimed uniform remainder. [given, F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Consider the bounded scalar multiplicative-noise SDE $dX_t=\sin(X_t)\,dW_t$ with $X_0=\pi/4$, and initialize the numerical method with $Y_0=X_0$. Fix $T>0$ and an integer $N\ge1$ with $h=T/N\le1$, and use the uniform grid $t_n=nh$ for $0\le n\le N$. At the state $Y_0=\pi/4$, its first Milstein step is
$$Y_1=\frac\pi4+\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\Delta W_0+\frac14((\Delta W_0)^2-h).$$
Unlike additive noise, the diffusion derivative contributes a nonzero centered correction. The hypotheses of the strong-order theorem apply to this coefficient field.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; a filtered probability space whose filtration satisfies the usual conditions; and a standard Brownian motion $W$ adapted to that filtration such that $W_t-W_s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and has law $N(0,t-s)$ for every $0\le s<t$ (for example, the usual augmentation of the natural filtration of $W$), as required by [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]; the SDE initial value $X_0=\pi/4\in L^2$ and matching numerical initial value $Y_0=X_0$; and a fixed horizon $T>0$ with an integer $N\ge1$, the uniform grid $t_n=nh$ for $0\le n\le N$, and $h=T/N\le1$.

[F1] [[def-milstein-scheme-and-iterated-integrals]]: for scalar noise, the increment contains $\frac12\sigma(Y_n)\sigma'(Y_n)((\Delta W_n)^2-h)$.

[F2] [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]: if $\Delta W_n\sim N(0,h)$, then its first, second, third and fourth moments are $0,h,0,3h^2$.

[L1] [[thm-commutative-milstein-strong-order-one]]: for coefficients in $C_b^3$ under the stated Brownian hypotheses, the grid root-mean-square error is $O(h)$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC is inherited through the Brownian/strong-Milstein interface [L1].

## Verification

**Given:** The assumptions above.

1.1 Here $b(x)=0$, $\sigma(x)=\sin x$, and $\sigma'(x)=\cos x$. At $Y_0=\pi/4$, both $\sigma(Y_0)$ and $\sigma'(Y_0)$ equal $1/\sqrt2$, so [F1] gives the stated update with correction coefficient $\frac12(1/\sqrt2)^2=1/4$. The function $\sin x$ and its derivatives through order three are bounded and continuous, so it meets the regularity premise of [L1]. [F1, L1, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F2], the correction has conditional mean $\frac14(h-h)=0$ and variance $\frac1{16}(3h^2-2h^2+h^2)=h^2/8$. Its covariance with the linear noise term is $\frac{1}{4\sqrt2}\mathbb E[(\Delta W_0)^3-h\Delta W_0]=0$. Hence the one-step increment variance is $h/2+h^2/8$, and the derivative correction is a separate nonzero fluctuation. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Applying [L1] to the SDE with $b=0$ and $\sigma(x)=\sin x$ yields $\max_{0\le n\le N}\mathbb E|Y_n-X_{t_n}|^2\le C_T h^2$, with $C_T$ independent of $N$, on the supplied uniform grid. Taking square roots yields grid root-mean-square error $O(h)$ on every fixed finite horizon. This is the theorem's bounded-coefficient multiplicative-noise case under the inherited AC convention [A1]; it supplies no weak-order-two statement for Heun. [L1, A1, given] ∎

      url: "https://stevencjxie8.com/files/refs/ref7.pdf"

## Example

Consider the bounded scalar multiplicative-noise SDE $dX_t=\sin(X_t)\,dW_t$ with $X_0=\pi/4$, and initialize the numerical method with $Y_0=X_0$. Fix $T>0$ and an integer $N\ge1$ with $h=T/N\le1$, and use the uniform grid $t_n=nh$ for $0\le n\le N$. At the state $Y_0=\pi/4$, its first Milstein step is
$$Y_1=\frac\pi4+\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\Delta W_0+\frac14((\Delta W_0)^2-h).$$
Unlike additive noise, the diffusion derivative contributes a nonzero centered correction. The hypotheses of the strong-order theorem apply to this coefficient field.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; a filtered probability space whose filtration satisfies the usual conditions; and a standard Brownian motion $W$ adapted to that filtration such that $W_t-W_s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and has law $N(0,t-s)$ for every $0\le s<t$ (for example, the usual augmentation of the natural filtration of $W$), as required by [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]; the SDE initial value $X_0=\pi/4\in L^2$ and matching numerical initial value $Y_0=X_0$; and a fixed horizon $T>0$ with an integer $N\ge1$, the uniform grid $t_n=nh$ for $0\le n\le N$, and $h=T/N\le1$.

[F1] [[def-milstein-scheme-and-iterated-integrals]]: for scalar noise, the increment contains $\frac12\sigma(Y_n)\sigma'(Y_n)((\Delta W_n)^2-h)$.

[F2] [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]: if $\Delta W_n\sim N(0,h)$, then its first, second, third and fourth moments are $0,h,0,3h^2$.

[L1] [[thm-commutative-milstein-strong-order-one]]: for coefficients in $C_b^3$ under the stated Brownian hypotheses, the grid root-mean-square error is $O(h)$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC is inherited through the Brownian/strong-Milstein interface [L1].

## Verification

**Given:** The assumptions above.

1.1 Here $b(x)=0$, $\sigma(x)=\sin x$, and $\sigma'(x)=\cos x$. At $Y_0=\pi/4$, both $\sigma(Y_0)$ and $\sigma'(Y_0)$ equal $1/\sqrt2$, so [F1] gives the stated update with correction coefficient $\frac12(1/\sqrt2)^2=1/4$. The function $\sin x$ and its derivatives through order three are bounded and continuous, so it meets the regularity premise of [L1]. [F1, L1, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F2], the correction has conditional mean $\frac14(h-h)=0$ and variance $\frac1{16}(3h^2-2h^2+h^2)=h^2/8$. Its covariance with the linear noise term is $\frac{1}{4\sqrt2}\mathbb E[(\Delta W_0)^3-h\Delta W_0]=0$. Hence the one-step increment variance is $h/2+h^2/8$, and the derivative correction is a separate nonzero fluctuation. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Applying [L1] to the SDE with $b=0$ and $\sigma(x)=\sin x$ yields $\max_{0\le n\le N}\mathbb E|Y_n-X_{t_n}|^2\le C_T h^2$, with $C_T$ independent of $N$, on the supplied uniform grid. Taking square roots yields grid root-mean-square error $O(h)$ on every fixed finite horizon. This is the theorem's bounded-coefficient multiplicative-noise case under the inherited AC convention [A1]; it supplies no weak-order-two statement for Heun. [L1, A1, given] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, $T>0$, and let $b,\sigma,\xi,W$ satisfy
the coefficient, Brownian, and initial-moment hypotheses of
[[thm-superlinear-sde-global-existence-and-moments]]. For each integer
$N\ge\max(1,\lceil T\rceil)$, put $h=T/N$ and define $Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$ by
[[alg-tamed-euler-superlinear-drift]]. Then for every finite $p\ge1$,
$$\sup_{N\ge\max(1,\lceil T\rceil)}\ \max_{0\le n\le N}\mathbb E|Y_n|^p<\infty.$$
The bound may depend on $p,T$, the coefficient constants, and the initial
moments, but not on $N$ or $n$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the autonomous coefficient and initial-moment hypotheses in the Statement; and the deterministic grid $t_n=nh$.

[F1] The tamed update is $Y_{n+1}=Y_n+h\,b(Y_n)/(1+h|b(Y_n)|)+\sigma(Y_n)\Delta W_n$; in particular $|h\,b(Y_n)/(1+h|b(Y_n)|)|\le1$. [[alg-tamed-euler-superlinear-drift]]

[F2] The sampled filtration $(\mathcal F_{t_n})_{n=0}^N$ is increasing. [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]

[F3] Each increment $\Delta W_n$ is independent of $\mathcal F_{t_n}$ and has law $N_m(0,hI_m)$. [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]]

[F4] For a nonnegative submartingale $Z$ and $r>1$, $\|\max_{k\le N}Z_k\|_r\le r/(r-1)\,\|Z_N\|_r$. [[thm-doob-lp-maximal-inequality]]

[F5] The coordinates of $\Delta W_n$ are independent $N(0,h)$ variables by [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]. Their density gives, for $2ah<1$, $\mathbb E e^{a|\Delta W_n|^2}=(1-2ah)^{-m/2}$: in one coordinate, integrate $(2\pi h)^{-1/2}e^{-(1/(2h)-a)x^2}$ and rescale to the normalized Gaussian density. The same density and $x=\sqrt h\,u$ show $\mathbb E|\Delta W_n|^r=h^{r/2}\mathbb E|G|^r<\infty$ for every finite $r$, where $G\sim N_m(0,I_m)$.

[F6] For predictable $G$ and $p\ge2$, $\|\sup_{t\le T}|\int_0^tG_s\,dW_s|\|_p \le C_{p,d}\| (\int_0^T\|G_s\|_F^2ds)^{1/2}\|_p$. [[lem-brownian-ito-integral-bdg-moment-bound]]

[F7] Hölder's inequality yields the $L^r$ triangle inequality for $r\ge1$, the three-factor bound $\mathbb E|UVW|\le(\mathbb E|U|^3\mathbb E|V|^3\mathbb E|W|^3)^{1/3}$, and $\mathbb E[1_A|Z|^p]\le\mathbb P(A)^{1/2}(\mathbb E|Z|^{2p})^{1/2}$. [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]] [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]]

[F8] For a nonnegative random variable $Z$ and $a>0$, $\mathbb P(Z\ge a)\le\mathbb E Z/a$. [[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]]

[F9] For a finite family of events, the probability of their union is at most the sum of their probabilities. [[thm-finite-union-bound]]

[A1] AC is inherited through the Brownian, normal, filtration, and Itô interfaces; the estimates below use only countable grid constructions. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and suppliers in the Statement and Facts.

1.1 The derivative bound, integrated on the segment from $0$ to $x$, gives $|b(x)|\le B(1+|x|^{q+1})$ for a finite $B$. One-sided Lipschitzness with $y=0$ gives $\langle x,b(x)\rangle\le B(1+|x|^2)$, and global Lipschitzness of $\sigma$ gives $\|\sigma(x)\|_F\le B(1+|x|)$. Increase $B$ so these bounds hold with one constant. For $|x|\ge1$ they imply $\|\sigma(x)\|_F^2\le B_1|x|^2$, $\langle x,b(x)\rangle\le B_1|x|^2$, and $|b(x)|^2\le B_1|x|^{2q+2}$. Thus, whenever $1\le|x|\le N^{1/(2q)}$ and $h=T/N$, $h^2|b(x)|^2\le B_1T h|x|^2$. Fix once and for all $\Lambda\ge\max\{1,2B_1(1+T),1+\sup_{|x|\le1}(|b(x)|+\|\sigma(x)\|_F)\}$; continuity and compactness make this choice finite. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 The recursion and Brownian adaptedness show by induction that $Y_k$ is $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable for every $k$. For $0\le k<N$, define $$\alpha_k=1_{\{|Y_k|\ge1\}}\frac{\langle Y_k,\sigma(Y_k)\Delta W_k\rangle}{|Y_k|^2},\qquad S_0=0,\quad S_j=\sum_{k<j}\alpha_k\ (1\le j\le N).$$ Since $\alpha_k$ is $\mathcal F_{t_{k+1}}$-measurable, $(S_j)$ is adapted to the sampled filtration. For $0\le n\le N$, also define $$D_n=(\Lambda+|\xi|) \exp\!\left(\Lambda T+ \max_{0\le u\le n}\sum_{k=u}^{n-1} (\Lambda h+\Lambda|\Delta W_k|^2+\alpha_k)\right).$$ On $|Y_k|\ge1$, write $\alpha_k=v_k\cdot\Delta W_k$ with $v_k=\sigma(Y_k)^{\mathsf T}Y_k/|Y_k|^2$; global Lipschitzness of $\sigma$ gives $|v_k|\le\|\sigma(Y_k)\|_F/|Y_k|\le C$. Conditionally on $\mathcal F_{t_k}$ its variance is $h|v_k|^2\le C^2h$; on $|Y_k|<1$, $\alpha_k=0$. Brownian independence and the Gaussian density therefore give $\mathbb E[\alpha_k\mid\mathcal F_{t_k}]=0$ and, by completing the square in each coordinate, $$\mathbb E[e^{r\alpha_k}\mid\mathcal F_{t_k}]\le e^{C^2r^2h/2}\qquad(r\in\mathbb R).$$ Conditional Jensen shows that $e^{QS_j}$ and $e^{-QS_j}$ are nonnegative submartingales for each $Q>0$. Iterating the preceding bound with $r=2Q$ gives terminal second moments at most $e^{2C^2Q^2T}$ for both processes. Doob's $L^2$ inequality [F4] then gives $\sup_N\mathbb E e^{Q\max_{j\le N}|S_j|}<\infty$: the exponential of the maximum is bounded by the sum of the maxima of $e^{QS_j}$ and $e^{-QS_j}$, whose expectations are bounded by their $L^2$ maxima. For any $r>0$, choose $Q\ge\max(1,r)$; since $x^{r/Q}\le1+x$ for $x\ge0$, this also bounds $\sup_N\mathbb E e^{r\max_{j\le N}|S_j|}$. Finally, for $N\ge4r\Lambda T$, [F5] and $-\log(1-u)\le2u$ on $0\le u\le1/2$ give $$\mathbb E\exp\!\left(r\Lambda\sum_{k<N}|\Delta W_k|^2\right)=\prod_{k<N}(1-2r\Lambda h)^{-m/2}\le e^{2rm\Lambda T}.$$ Every suffix sum $\sum_{k=u}^{j-1}\alpha_k=S_j-S_u$ is bounded in absolute value by $2\max_{i\le N}|S_i|$. Since $$\max_{n\le N}D_n^p\le(\Lambda+|\xi|)^p e^{2p\Lambda T}\exp\!\left(p\Lambda\sum_{k<N}|\Delta W_k|^2+2p\max_{j\le N}|S_j|\right),$$ the three-factor Hölder bound [F7], the all-moment assumption on $\xi$, the square-exponential estimate with $r=3p$, and the exponential-martingale bound with $r=6p$ give a uniform moment for $\max_{n\le N}D_n^p$ when $N\ge N_0(p):=\max\{1,\lceil T\rceil,\lceil12p\Lambda T\rceil\}$. The finitely many smaller $N$ will be handled separately. [F2, F3, F4, F5, F7, given]

1.3 Set $a_n=(\mathbb E|Y_n|^p)^{1/p}$ for $p\ge2$. Decompose the recursion as $$Y_n=\xi+\sum_{k<n}h b_h(Y_k)+\sigma(0)W_{t_n} +\sum_{k<n}(\sigma(Y_k)-\sigma(0))\Delta W_k.$$ The drift sum has norm at most $N$ by [F1]. The last sum is a continuous Brownian Itô integral with a predictable step integrand. By [F6], global Lipschitzness of $\sigma$, and the $L^{p/2}$ triangle inequality from [F7], its $L^p$ norm is at most $$C_p\left(\sum_{k<n}h\, \|\sigma(Y_k)-\sigma(0)\|_{L^p}^2\right)^{1/2} \le C_p\left(h\sum_{k<n}a_k^2\right)^{1/2}.$$ The pointwise inequality $|u_1+\cdots+u_4|^p\le 4^{p-1}\sum_i|u_i|^p$ and the bounded $p$th moments of $W_t$ on $[0,T]$ therefore give $$a_n^2\le C_p(1+\|\xi\|_{L^p}^2+N^2) +C_ph\sum_{k<n}a_k^2.$$ Iterating this finite recurrence yields $\max_{n\le N}a_n^2\le C_p(1+\|\xi\|_{L^p}^2+N^2)e^{C_pT}$, hence $\max_{n\le N}\|Y_n\|_{L^p}\le C_p(1+N)$. [F1, F3, F6, F7, given, algebra]

2.1 Write $\Delta W_k=W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k}$ and use $\alpha_k,D_n$ from step 1.2. Define $$\Omega_n=\left\{\max_{k<n}D_k\le N^{1/(2q)},\ \max_{k<n}|\Delta W_k|\le1\right\}.$$ On $|Y_k|\le1$ and $|\Delta W_k|\le1$, [F1] gives $|Y_{k+1}|\le1+h|b(Y_k)|+\|\sigma(Y_k)\|_F\le\Lambda$. On $1\le|Y_k|\le N^{1/(2q)}$, expand the squared update. The drift cross term is at most $2B_1h|Y_k|^2$; the squared taming increment is at most $B_1Th|Y_k|^2$ by step 1.1; the diffusion square is at most $B_1|Y_k|^2|\Delta W_k|^2$; and the drift-noise cross term is at most the sum of those two square terms. The remaining cross term is exactly $2|Y_k|^2\alpha_k$. With the fixed $\Lambda$ chosen in step 1.1 large enough for these coefficients, $1+u\le e^u$ therefore gives $$|Y_{k+1}|\le |Y_k| \exp(\Lambda h+\Lambda|\Delta W_k|^2+\alpha_k).$$ Induction on $n$, starting either from $Y_0=\xi$ or from the last index with $|Y_k|\le1$, now gives $1_{\Omega_n}|Y_n|\le D_n$: the first step after such an index is at most $\Lambda$, and the later factors are bounded by the suffix sum in $D_n$. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, given, algebra, construct]

2.2 Markov's inequality [F8] and step 1.2 imply, for any $r>0$, $$\mathbb P\!\left(\max_{n\le N}D_n>N^{1/(2q)}\right) \le N^{-r/(2q)}\mathbb E\max_{n\le N}D_n^r.$$ Also, by the finite union bound [F9] and the $r$th Gaussian moment, $\mathbb P(\max_{k<N}|\Delta W_k|>1) \le C_rN h^{r/2}=C_{r,T}N^{1-r/2}$. Choosing $r$ arbitrarily large in these bounds shows that for every $s>0$ there is $C_s$ with $\mathbb P(\Omega_N^c)\le C_sN^{-s}$ for all $N$. [F3, F5, F8, F9, step 1.2, given, algebra]

3.1 For $p\ge1$, on $\Omega_N$ step 2.1 bounds $\mathbb E[1_{\Omega_N}|Y_n|^p]\le\mathbb E D_n^p\le C_p$; here $\Omega_N\subseteq\Omega_n$. On the complement, [F7] and step 1.3 give $$\mathbb E[1_{\Omega_N^c}|Y_n|^p] \le\mathbb P(\Omega_N^c)^{1/2} \|Y_n\|_{L^{2p}}^p \le C_sN^{-s/2}(1+N)^p.$$ Choose $s>2p$. This is uniformly bounded. For the finitely many small $N$ excluded in step 1.2, the finite recursion and linear growth of $\sigma$ give finite moments by induction; taking their finite maximum completes the uniform bound. For $1\le p<2$, apply Hölder on the probability space to the $p=2$ result. AC is exactly [A1]. [A1, F1, F7, step 2.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice.

For the LQR data of [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]], let $\mathcal F$ be nonempty and convex and let $u\in\mathcal F$. Put $g(t)=B(t)^Tp(t)+R(t)u(t)$, with the adjoint from [[def-ctrl1-lqr-adjoint-equation]]. If $u$ minimizes $J$ on $\mathcal F$, then
$$\int_0^T g(t)^T(v(t)-u(t))\,dt\ge0\qquad(v\in\mathcal F).$$
Conversely, if this variational inequality holds at $u$, then $u$ is the unique minimizer on $\mathcal F$.

If $\mathcal F=\mathcal U_c$, the variational inequality is equivalent (under Dependent Choice, hence Countable Choice) to the existence of one null set $N$ such that $g(t)^T(c-u(t))\ge0$ for every $t\notin N$ and every $c\in U_c$. The pointwise condition is not asserted for additional state or terminal constraints.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The LQR data, a nonempty convex feasible set $\mathcal F$, a control $u\in\mathcal F$, its continuous adjoint, and the variational-inequality hypothesis when proving sufficiency or the reverse pointwise implication.

[F1] The objective has bounded first-order map $DJ(u)[w]=\int_0^T(B^Tp+Ru)^Tw\,dt$, with remainder $O(\|w\|_2^2)$ ([[lem-ctrl1-lqr-adjoint-identity-and-gradient]]).

[F2] The state map is affine, and for every $u,v\in L^2$ the quadratic expansion has the exact remainder $J(v)-J(u)-DJ(u)[v-u]=\frac12\int_0^T(\delta x^TQ\delta x+(v-u)^TR(v-u))dt+\frac12\delta x(T)^TP\delta x(T)$, where $\delta x=x_v-x_u$ ([[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]], [[lem-ctrl1-measurable-linear-ode-state-map]]).

[F3] Cauchy–Schwarz makes the integral pairing finite for $L^2$ factors ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]).

[A1] Dependent Choice and Countable Choice are available for the countable dense subset of $U_c$ used in the pointwise equivalence ([[def-dependent-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[lem-dependent-choice-implies-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

1.1 Suppose $u$ minimizes $J$ on $\mathcal F$ and fix $v\in\mathcal F$. Convexity gives $u_\theta=u+\theta(v-u)\in\mathcal F$ for $0\le\theta\le1$. Hence $(J(u_\theta)-J(u))/\theta\ge0$ for $0<\theta\le1$. The first-order expansion [F1] with increment $\theta(v-u)$ has quotient $DJ(u)[v-u]+O(\theta\|v-u\|_2^2)$, so its limit is $DJ(u)[v-u]$. This proves the displayed variational inequality. [F1, given, choose, algebra]

1.2 Suppose the pointwise inequalities hold outside one null set and $\mathcal F=\mathcal U_c$. For any $v\in\mathcal U_c$, substitute $c=v(t)$ outside that null set and the null set on which $v(t)\notin U_c$. The vector $g=B^Tp+Ru$ lies in $L^2$ because $B,R$ are essentially bounded, $p$ is continuous on the compact horizon, and $u\in L^2$; [F3] makes $g^T(v-u)$ integrable. Integrating proves the global variational inequality. [F3, given, algebra]

1.3 Assume the variational inequality at $u$. For any $v\in\mathcal F$, [F2] and $Q\succeq0$, $R\succeq rI$ give $J(v)-J(u)\ge DJ(u)[v-u]+\frac r2\|v-u\|_2^2$. The linear term is nonnegative by the assumed inequality; hence $J(v)\ge J(u)$, with strict inequality if $v\ne u$. Thus $u$ is the unique minimizer. [F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Assume the global variational inequality and suppose no common null set makes all pointwise inequalities true. Construct a countable dense $D\subseteq U_c$ by choosing, using [A1], one point from each rational open ball that meets $U_c$; the countable base property makes the chosen set dense. Define $M=\bigcup_{d\in D,k\ge1}E_{d,k}$, where $E_{d,k}=\{t:g(t)^T(d-u(t))\le-1/k\}$. This is measurable. Continuity in $c$ and density show that $M$ is exactly the set where some $c\in U_c$ violates the pointwise inequality, so the absence of a common null set means $|M|>0$. Countability implies some $E_{d,k}$ has positive measure. Put $v(t)=d$ on that set and $v(t)=u(t)$ elsewhere. This measurable control lies in $\mathcal U_c$, but $\int_0^Tg^T(v-u)dt\le-|E_{d,k}|/k<0$, contradicting the assumed global variational inequality. Therefore one null set suffices for every $c\in U_c$. [A1, given, choose, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

For arbitrary active state or terminal constraints the valid first-order condition is the integral inequality over the feasible set. The multiplier $p$ in the unconstrained adjoint equation alone does not encode normal multipliers for those additional constraints.

## Statement

Let $\Lambda$ be finite, contain $0$, and let the real basis
$(\psi_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\Lambda}$ be as in
[[def-chaos-orthonormal-tensor-basis]]. For real $u\in L^2(\rho)$ set
$c_\alpha=\langle u,\psi_\alpha\rangle$ and
$P_\Lambda u=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}c_\alpha\psi_\alpha$ as in
[[def-finite-chaos-orthogonal-projection]]. Then
$$\|u\|_{L^2(\rho)}^2=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}c_\alpha^2+
\|u-P_\Lambda u\|_{L^2(\rho)}^2.$$
The residual is orthogonal to $\mathcal P_\Lambda$,
$\mathbb E[u]=c_0$, and
$$\operatorname{Var}(u)=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda\setminus\{0\}}c_\alpha^2+
\|u-P_\Lambda u\|_{L^2(\rho)}^2.$$
Here $\operatorname{Var}(u)=\mathbb E[(u-\mathbb E u)^2]$; no completeness of
the polynomial family is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite real orthonormal polynomial family containing $\psi_0=1$ and $u\in L^2(\rho)$.

[F1] [[def-finite-chaos-orthogonal-projection]] defines $c_\alpha$ and $P_\Lambda u$ by the displayed finite sum.

[F2] [[thm-independent-polynomial-chaos-tensors-are-orthonormal]] gives $\langle\psi_\alpha,\psi_\beta\rangle=\delta_{\alpha\beta}$ and $\psi_0=1$.

[F3] [[def-finite-chaos-orthogonal-projection]] establishes the choice-free integral inner product and its norm-square identity; bilinearity and symmetry give the finite orthogonal norm identities by expansion, without completeness.

## Proof

1.1 For each $\beta\in\Lambda$, bilinearity and [F2] give $\langle u-P_\Lambda u,\psi_\beta\rangle =c_\beta-\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}c_\alpha\delta_{\alpha\beta}=0$. Thus the residual is orthogonal to every basis vector and hence to their finite span. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Write $u=P_\Lambda u+(u-P_\Lambda u)$. By step 1.1 the two terms are orthogonal, so bilinearity and symmetry from [F3] give $\|u\|_2^2=\|P_\Lambda u\|_2^2+\|u-P_\Lambda u\|_2^2$. Expanding the finite sum with [F2] gives $\|P_\Lambda u\|_2^2=\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in\Lambda}c_\alpha c_\beta\delta_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}c_\alpha^2$. $$\operatorname{Var}(u)=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda\setminus\{0\}}c_\alpha^2+

$$0\le n_i(t)\le M/x_i,\qquad 0\le L(t)\le M,\qquad M_2(t)\le M_{2,0}+t\left[K_*M^2+\Delta^2\left(\frac{K_*M^2}{8a^2}+\frac{\beta_*DM}{4a}\right)\right],$$

[F3] [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]]: every locally Lipschitz finite-dimensional initial-value problem has a unique maximal solution.

## Statement

Let $\mu_t$ be a continuous solution on $[0,T]$ with initial mass $M_1$, and let $\nu_t^R$ be the retained measure of the finite sectional system initialized by retaining the projection $P_\Delta\mu_0$ on pivots at most $R$ and placing the projected tail mass $\int_{(R,\infty)}x\,P_\Delta\mu_0(dx)$ in its reported reservoir. Assume $R$ is a pivot endpoint and $\Delta\le1$. Then
$$d_{BL}(\nu_t^R,\mu_t)\le e^{C_Tt}\left[C_QT\Delta+\frac{\Delta}{2}M_0(\mu_t)+\frac{M_1}{R}+\frac{2K_*M_1^2t}{aR}\right],\qquad 0\le t\le T,$$
where $C_Q$ is from [[lem-fixed-pivot-coagulation-fragmentation-quadrature-error]], $C_T$ is a finite bounded-number stability constant, and the terms proportional to $\Delta$, $R^{-1}$ are respectively the grid and cutoff errors. The reservoir itself is diagnostic and does not recreate the omitted transition law.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The continuous weak model, the finite reported-overflow scheme, and the no-cutoff pivot comparison.

[F1] [[def-continuous-size-coagulation-fragmentation-weak-model]]: the continuous population satisfies the weak coagulation-fragmentation equation.

[F2] [[def-conservative-fixed-pivot-redistribution]]: in-range sizes are redistributed by positive barycentric weights and above-cutoff products enter a mass reservoir.

[F3] [[alg-finite-sectional-coagulation-fragmentation-balance]]: the finite algorithm applies the in-range pivot rule and omits retained particles for products above $R$.

[F4] [[thm-continuous-coagulation-fragmentation-moment-bounds]]: $M_1$ is constant and $M_0$ is bounded on $[0,T]$.

[F5] [[thm-infinite-fixed-pivot-sectional-grid-error]]: the unbounded-pivot flow differs from $\mu_t$ by at most $e^{C_Tt}C_QT\Delta+(\Delta/2)M_0(\mu_t)$.

[F6] [[lem-cutoff-overflow-return-error-bound]]: replacing the unbounded-pivot flow by the finite reported-overflow flow adds at most $e^{C_Tt}[M_1/R+2K_*M_1^2t/(aR)]$.

## Proof

1.1 By [F1] the target is a continuous-model solution; [F2]–[F3] specify that finite products above $R$ leave the retained measure and enter only the diagnostic reservoir. Form the unbounded-pivot solution $\eta_t$ from the initial projection $P_\Delta\mu_0$. Split the difference as
$$d_{BL}(\nu_t^R,\mu_t)\le d_{BL}(\nu_t^R,\eta_t)+d_{BL}(\eta_t,\mu_t).$$
This is the triangle inequality for the discrepancy in [F1]. [given, F1, F2, F3]

1.2 Apply [F5] to the second term and [F6] to the first term. Their stated bounds use the same conserved initial mass $M_1$ and finite-horizon number bound, so taking a common stability constant $C_T$ and adding gives exactly the displayed estimate. The first two contributions vanish with grid spacing, and the last two with cutoff growth. [given, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $d\ge1$, let $f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and use a level
hierarchy as in [[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]]. Suppose its tensor
rules satisfy $Q_L^{\otimes d}(f)\to I_d(f)$ and its detail family is absolutely
summable in the sense of [[def-smolyak-absolute-detail-summability]]. For every
finite downward-closed $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d$ containing $0$,
$$|I_d(f)-Q_\Lambda(f)|\le\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb N_0^d\setminus\Lambda}|\delta_\ell(f)|.$$
In particular, the dyadic composite-Simpson hierarchy satisfies the convergence
hypothesis for continuous $f$ by
[[lem-smolyak-dyadic-tensor-simpson-convergence]], and for the mixed-derivative
class of [[lem-smolyak-mixed-simpson-detail-decay]] the same hierarchy also
satisfies absolute summability.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A dimension $d\ge1$, continuous $f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R$, a level hierarchy whose tensor rules converge on $f$ to $I_d(f)$, absolute summability of its detail family, and a finite downward-closed $\Lambda$ containing $0$.

[F1] [[def-smolyak-cubature]]: $Q_\Lambda(f)$ is the finite sum of the tensor details indexed by $\Lambda$.

[F2] [[def-smolyak-absolute-detail-summability]]: a nonnegative multi-index sum is the supremum of its finite subsums when these are bounded; the omitted tail uses the same definition on the complement of $\Lambda$.

[F3] [[lem-smolyak-rectangular-telescope]]: the sum of details over $R_L=\{\ell:0\le\ell_j\le L\}$ is $Q_L^{\otimes d}$.

[F4] [[lem-smolyak-dyadic-tensor-simpson-convergence]]: $Q_L^{\otimes d}(f)\to I_d(f)$.

[F5] [[lem-triangle-inequality-finite]]: the absolute value of each finite detail sum is at most the sum of its absolute terms.

[F6] [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]: finite sums split over disjoint finite index sets.

[F7] [[def-real-limit]]: convergence of a real sequence is tested using every positive rational tolerance.

[F8] [[lem-of-triangle-inequality]]: $|x+y|\le|x|+|y|$ for real $x,y$.

[F9] [[lem-smolyak-mixed-simpson-detail-decay]]: under its continuous mixed fourth-derivative hypotheses, every finite absolute-detail subsum has the common finite bound $\sum_{S\subseteq[d]}M_S(17/43200)^{|S|}$.

[F10] [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]: below every positive real lies a positive rational.

## Proof

1.1 Choose $L$ large enough that $\Lambda\subseteq R_L$. By [F1], [F3], and [F6], $Q_L^{\otimes d}(f)-Q_\Lambda(f)=\sum_{\ell\in R_L\setminus\Lambda}\delta_\ell(f)$. The index set on the right is finite and is contained in $\mathbb N_0^d\setminus\Lambda$. [given, F1, F3, F6, choose]

2.1 By [F5] and [F2], the absolute value of the right side in step 1.1 is at most the omitted-detail tail $T_\Lambda:=\sum_{\ell\notin\Lambda}|\delta_\ell(f)|$ for every sufficiently large $L$. Put $x_L:=Q_L^{\otimes d}(f)-Q_\Lambda(f)$ and $z:=I_d(f)-Q_\Lambda(f)$; the convergence hypothesis in **Given** says $|x_L-z|=|Q_L^{\otimes d}(f)-I_d(f)|$ is eventually below every positive rational tolerance. If $|z|>T_\Lambda$, [F10] supplies a positive rational $\varepsilon$ with $2\varepsilon<|z|-T_\Lambda$. For sufficiently large $L$, both $\Lambda\subseteq R_L$ and $|x_L-z|<\varepsilon$ hold by finiteness of $\Lambda$ and [F7]. The triangle inequality [F8] then gives $|x_L|\ge |z|-|x_L-z|>|z|-\varepsilon>T_\Lambda$, contradicting the preceding tail bound. Hence the displayed omitted-tail inequality holds. [given, F2, F5, F7, F8, F10, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For the dyadic composite-Simpson hierarchy, [F4] supplies the convergence hypothesis in **Given**. If the mixed-derivative hypotheses of [F9] hold, its common bound makes the finite subsums of $\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb N_0^d}|\delta_\ell(f)|$ bounded above. By the definition [F2], the full absolute-detail sum is therefore defined and finite, so step 2.1 applies and proves the stated particular error case. [given, F2, F4, F9, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ be Hermitian positive definite and use its pattern from [[def-hermitian-structural-graph-adapter]]. The local Hermitian Schur-support lemma [[lem-hermitian-schur-support-is-contained-in-structural-fill]] applies. In exact arithmetic, the Cholesky recurrence in [[alg-sparse-cholesky-with-invalid-pivot-status]] returns the unique factor $L$ satisfying $PAP^*=LL^*$ and positive diagonal, and every nonzero strict-lower entry of $L$ is permitted by the filled graph $G^+_\pi$.

For $i>j$ with $\{i,j\}\in E^+_\pi$ (where ordered position $i$ represents original vertex $v_i$), define the recurrence numerator
$$\nu_{ij}=B_{ij}-\sum_{k<j}l_{ik}\overline{l_{jk}},\qquad B=PAP^*.$$
If $\nu_{ij}\ne0$ at every permitted strict-lower position, then the numerical nonzero pattern of $L$ is exactly the lower-triangular part of $G^+_\pi$ together with its diagonal. Without this no-cancellation hypothesis only the upper-pattern inclusion is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions


**Given:** A Hermitian positive-definite matrix $A$, the stated batch-2 graph/ordering interface, and its Schur-support hypothesis.

[F1] [[alg-sparse-cholesky-with-invalid-pivot-status]]: The permutation matrix has row $j$ equal to row $v_j$ of $I_n$, and the exact algorithm uses $d_j=B_{jj}-\sum_{k<j}|l_{jk}|^2$, $l_{jj}=\sqrt{d_j}$, and $l_{ij}=(B_{ij}-\sum_{k<j}l_{ik}\overline{l_{jk}})/l_{jj}$ on filled positions.

[F2] [[lem-hermitian-schur-support-is-contained-in-structural-fill]]: With nonzero scalar pivots, each Hermitian Schur complement is supported inside the Hermitian filled graph.

[F3] [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]: A Hermitian positive-definite matrix has a unique factorization $C=RR^*$ with $R$ lower triangular and positive real diagonal.

## Proof


1.1 A permutation preserves positive definiteness: for $x\ne0$, $P^*x\ne0$ and $x^*Bx=(P^*x)^*A(P^*x)>0$. Thus [F3] gives a unique exact Cholesky factor $R$ of $B$. [given, F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 We show the recurrence in [F1] recovers $R$ column by column, beginning with $j=0$ where the sum is empty. From $B=RR^*$, its $(j,j)$ entry is $B_{jj}=\sum_{k<j}|r_{jk}|^2+|r_{jj}|^2$; since $r_{jj}>0$, the computed exact pivot is $d_j=|r_{jj}|^2>0$ and its positive square root is $r_{jj}$. [step 1.1, F1, F3, base, algebra]

3.1 For $i>j$, the $(i,j)$ entry of $B=RR^*$ is $B_{ij}=\sum_{k<j}r_{ik}\overline{r_{jk}}+r_{ij}\overline{r_{jj}}$. Because $r_{jj}>0$, solving this identity for $r_{ij}$ gives exactly the recurrence in [F1]. Induction on $j$ therefore makes every computed column equal to the corresponding column of $R$. [step 2.1, F1, IH, induction, algebra]

4.1 Let $S^j$ be the exact Schur complement after eliminating positions $0,\ldots,j-1$ from $B$. Initially $S^0=B$. If the first $j$ columns equal those of $R$, then [step 3.1, F1, F2, IH, induction, algebra]
$$S^j_{ab}=B_{ab}-\sum_{k<j}r_{ak}\overline{r_{bk}}.$$
This identity holds at $j=0$; eliminating pivot $j$ subtracts $r_{aj}\overline{r_{bj}}$ because $S^j_{jj}=r_{jj}^2$ and $S^j_{aj}=r_{aj}r_{jj}$, so it holds at $j+1$. In particular the recurrence numerator at position $(i,j)$ is $S^j_{ij}$. By [F2], a nonzero such entry can occur only on an edge of the filled graph. Therefore every structurally absent position has zero numerator and is correctly omitted, proving the factor support inclusion. [step 3.1, F1, F2, induction, algebra]

5.1 At each permitted strict-lower position, the recurrence gives $l_{ij}=\nu_{ij}/l_{jj}$ and step 2.1 gives $l_{jj}>0$. Hence $\nu_{ij}\ne0$ implies $l_{ij}\ne0$. Under the stated no-cancellation condition every permitted position is nonzero; together with step 4.1 this gives equality of patterns. [step 2.1, step 4.1, F1, algebra]

6.1 Steps 2.1 and 3.1 establish that the exact algorithm returns the unique Cholesky factor; step 4.1 proves the structural upper pattern in the complex Hermitian case; step 5.1 proves equality precisely under the no-cancellation hypothesis. No finite-precision success or stability claim follows from this exact-arithmetic theorem. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, discharge-induction] ∎

## Statement

For the SQP subproblem of [[def-sqp-linearized-quadratic-subproblem]] with
$B$ symmetric positive definite, the exact algorithm of
[[alg-sqp-exhaustive-active-set-qp-solve]] terminates after finitely many
subset tests. It returns `QP-infeasible` exactly when the subproblem's
polyhedron is empty; otherwise it returns the unique global minimizer, full
equality and inequality multiplier vectors, and the retained equality basis
$E$ and inequality support $J$ of its KKT certificate.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The exact-arithmetic algorithm and a subproblem with positive-
definite $B$.

[A1] The equality rows retained by the algorithm are independent and their
right-hand sides define the same consistent equality set as the original rows.

[F1] [[lem-sqp-convex-quadratic-subproblem-has-unique-kkt-certificate]]:
feasibility gives a unique minimizer with a KKT certificate supported on a
set of active rows independent together with the equality rows.

[F2] [[lem-sqp-kkt-matrix-nonsingularity-under-reduced-curvature]]: if the
active/equality rows are independent and $B$ is positive definite on their
null space, the KKT matrix is nonsingular.

[F3] [[alg-sqp-exhaustive-active-set-qp-solve]] tests every inequality subset
in a finite order and accepts only feasible candidates with nonnegative
selected inequality multipliers; it returns their multipliers expanded to the
original equality and inequality indices, together with $E$ and $J$.

## Proof

1.1 The equality reduction is finite: there are finitely many row subsets to check, and exact rank and consistency tests decide each one. Under [A1] it preserves the equality feasible set; if it reports inconsistency, that set is empty and the full QP is infeasible. [A1, F3, algebra]

1.2 For any enumerated subset whose rows are independent, the KKT matrix is nonsingular by [F2], because $B$ is positive definite on every subspace. If that candidate passes the inequality feasibility and multiplier-sign filters, its zero-extended multipliers give a feasible KKT tuple for the original QP, so [F1] identifies it with the unique global minimizer. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 If the QP is feasible, [F1] supplies an active KKT support whose rows are independent together with the reduced equality rows. [F3] therefore tests that support. The solve in step 1.2 returns its KKT point, and its feasibility and nonnegative multipliers make it pass both filters. Hence the algorithm cannot report `QP-infeasible` on a feasible subproblem. [A1, F1, F2, F3]

3.1 There are exactly $2^m$ inequality subsets. Every subset requires only finitely many exact rank, solve, and feasibility operations, so [F3] terminates. If no candidate was found, step 2.1 shows the QP is infeasible; if a candidate was found, step 1.2 shows it is the unique minimizer with the returned full KKT multipliers and support data. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

For every nonstationary trial of [[alg-trust-region-method]], the selected
predicted reduction is positive, and every accepted trial strictly decreases
the objective.

Assume the hypotheses and parameter ranges of
[[thm-trust-region-global-liminf-gradient]], and let $f_{inf}$ be a lower
bound for $f$. For each target $0<\varepsilon\le1$, run
[[alg-trust-region-method]] until its first iterate with
$\|\nabla f(x_k)\|_2\le\varepsilon$. Define
$$c_\delta:=\min\left\{\frac1{2M_B},
\frac{\theta_C(1-\eta_2)}{2(L+M_B)}\right\},\qquad
c_R:=\min\{\Delta_0,\gamma_{dec}\min\{c_\delta,\Delta_{max}\}\},$$
where a zero denominator means $+\infty$, and put
$$c_P:=\min\{c_R,1/M_B\},\qquad
c_S:=\tfrac12\eta_1\theta_Cc_P>0.$$
Then the number $N_s$ of accepted steps before reaching the target and the
number $N_u$ of rejected trials obey
$$N_s\le\frac{f(x_0)-f_{inf}}{c_S\varepsilon^2},$$
$$N_u\le\frac{\log(\Delta_0/r_\varepsilon)+N_s\log\gamma_{inc}}
{|\log\gamma_{dec}|},\qquad
r_\varepsilon:=\min\{\Delta_0,\gamma_{dec}\min\{c_\delta\varepsilon,
\Delta_{max}\}\}.$$
Here $\log$ denotes the natural logarithm of a positive real.
Consequently, accepted steps and total trials $N_s+N_u$ are
$O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. An outer cap at least
the resulting total-trial bound suffices for the finite-budget algorithm to
return `target-achieved` or `stationary`, with gradient norm at most
$\varepsilon$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The model-Hessian bound, gradient Lipschitz bound, bounded-below
objective, parameter ranges, and step safeguard of the trust-region method.

[F1] [[alg-trust-region-method]]: each step has predicted reduction at least
$\theta_C$ times the Cauchy decrease; a rejection multiplies $\Delta$ by
$\gamma_{dec}$; an accepted update multiplies it by a factor in
$[1,\gamma_{inc}]$, respecting $\Delta_{max}$.

[F2] [[lem-trust-region-cauchy-decrease]]: if $a:=\|g_k\|_2>0$, then
$$m_k(0)-m_k(p_C)\ge\tfrac12a\min\{\Delta_k,a/\|B_k\|_2\},$$
with the zero-matrix convention stated there.

[F3] [[lem-trust-region-ratio-accuracy-for-small-radii]]: when
$a\ge\varepsilon$ and $\Delta_k\le c_\delta\varepsilon$, the algorithm's
small-radius branch gives $\rho_k\ge\eta_2$ and uses the boundary Cauchy
step, so rejection is impossible.

[F4] [[def-natural-logarithm]]: $\log x$ is defined for $x>0$ as the inverse
of the real exponential.

[F5] [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: $\log$ is strictly increasing,
$\log1=0$, and the product and quotient laws hold for positive arguments.

[F6] [[lem-natural-logarithm-bounded-by-argument]]:
$0\le\log y\le y-1\le y$ for $y\ge1$.

[F7] [[thm-of-archimedean]]: for every real $R$ there is an integer
$m\in\mathbb N$ with $m>R$.

[F8] [[lem-geometric-sequence-null]]: if $0<q<1$, then $q^j\to0$ as
$j\to\infty$.

[A1] The target satisfies $0<\varepsilon\le1$.

[A2] Every model matrix is symmetric with norm at most $M_B$, and the
gradient is $L$-Lipschitz on every trial segment.

[A3] The objective satisfies $f(x)\ge f_{inf}$ at all iterates.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Let $\bar\delta_\varepsilon:=
\min\{c_\delta\varepsilon,\Delta_{max}\}$. Every radius during a
pre-target trial is at least
$$r_\varepsilon=\min\{\Delta_0,\gamma_{dec}\bar\delta_\varepsilon\}>0.$$
Indeed, this holds initially. If a trial is rejected, [F3] implies its
radius exceeded $\bar\delta_\varepsilon$, since at or below that threshold
the ratio is at least $\eta_2$; after multiplication by $\gamma_{dec}$ the
new radius is greater than $\gamma_{dec}\bar\delta_\varepsilon$. An
accepted update does not decrease the radius. Induction proves the bound.
[given, A1, A2, F1, F3, induction, algebra]

1.2 If the target were never reached, every rejection block would be finite:
an infinite block would multiply a fixed radius by $\gamma_{dec}^j\to0$ by
[F8], eventually making $\Delta\le\bar\delta_\varepsilon$, where [F3]
forbids rejection. Thus an infinite pre-target run would contain infinitely
many accepted trials. For any accepted trial its starting gradient norm
$a$ exceeds $\varepsilon$. From step 1.1,
$\Delta_k\ge r_\varepsilon\ge c_R\varepsilon$, because
$\varepsilon\le1$ and
$$\min\{c_\delta\varepsilon,\Delta_{max}\}
\ge\varepsilon\min\{c_\delta,\Delta_{max}\}.$$
Since $\Delta_0\ge\varepsilon\Delta_0$, taking the minimum with
$\Delta_0$ in the definition of $r_\varepsilon$ gives
$r_\varepsilon\ge c_R\varepsilon$.
Also $a/\|B_k\|_2\ge\varepsilon/M_B$, with the stated infinity
convention if $M_B=0$. Hence
$$\min\{\Delta_k,a/\|B_k\|_2\}\ge c_P\varepsilon.$$
By [F1] and [F2], the predicted reduction is at least
$\tfrac12\theta_Cc_P\varepsilon^2$. Acceptance gives actual decrease at
least $\eta_1$ times this amount, namely $c_S\varepsilon^2$. If the target
were never reached, after $m$ accepted trials the objective would be at most
$f(x_0)-m c_S\varepsilon^2$. By [F7] choose an integer
$m>(f(x_0)-f_{inf})/(c_S\varepsilon^2)$; this contradicts [A3]. Therefore
the target is reached after finitely many accepted trials. Summing their
decreases gives
$N_s c_S\varepsilon^2\le f(x_0)-f_{inf}$, the claimed successful-step
bound. [given, A1, A2, A3, F1, F2, F3, F7, F8, step 1.1, choose,
assume-contra, discharge-contradiction, algebra]

2.1 Let $\Delta_T$ be the radius after the accepted trial that first
reaches the target. Each rejected trial multiplies the radius by
$\gamma_{dec}$; each accepted update multiplies it by some
$r_j\in[1,\gamma_{inc}]$. Therefore
$$\Delta_T=\Delta_0\gamma_{dec}^{N_u}\prod_{j=1}^{N_s}r_j.$$
Step 1.1 gives $\Delta_T\ge r_\varepsilon$. By [F5],
$\log\gamma_{dec}<0$, and logarithms of positive products give
$$\log\Delta_T=\log\Delta_0+N_u\log\gamma_{dec}
+\sum_{j=1}^{N_s}\log r_j.$$
Rearranging and using $\log r_j\le\log\gamma_{inc}$ yields
$$N_u|\log\gamma_{dec}|
=\log(\Delta_0/\Delta_T)+\sum_{j=1}^{N_s}\log r_j
\le\log(\Delta_0/r_\varepsilon)+N_s\log\gamma_{inc},$$
which proves the rejection bound, including every rejected trial.
[given, F1, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Since $r_\varepsilon\ge c_R\varepsilon$ for
$0<\varepsilon\le1$, [F5] gives
$$\log(\Delta_0/r_\varepsilon)
\le\log(\Delta_0/(c_R\varepsilon))
=\log(\Delta_0/c_R)+\log(1/\varepsilon).$$
By [F6], $\log(1/\varepsilon)\le1/\varepsilon$; since
$0<\varepsilon\le1$, $1/\varepsilon\le1/\varepsilon^2$. Thus the radius
term is $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$, as is $N_s$ by step 1.2, so
$N_s+N_u=O(\varepsilon^{-2})$. If the finite outer cap
allows at least that many trials, the process reaches the target before the
cap. [given, F5, F6, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.1 For any nonstationary trial, $\|g_k\|_2>0$ and $\Delta_k>0$.
By [F2], the Cauchy step has $P_C>0$. The selection rule either chooses a
candidate with predicted decrease at least $\theta_C P_C$, or uses $p_C$;
the small-radius override also uses $p_C$. Since $0<\theta_C\le1$, every
branch therefore gives $P_k\ge\theta_C P_C>0$, so the ratio in the
algorithm is defined. [F1, F2, given, cases, algebra]

4.1 On an accepted trial, $\rho_k\ge\eta_1>0$ and $P_k>0$ by step 3.1.
Thus $f(x_{k+1})=f(x_k)-\rho_kP_k<f(x_k)$, proving strict decrease at every
accepted trial. [F1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

$A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]), and let $b,x_0\in\mathbb C^n$.
The complex scalars form a field ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]).
As additional input, take maps $\mathcal P_1,\ldots,\mathcal P_m:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$.
The maps may vary with $j$; no linearity or fixedness is assumed. In the usual
matrix case, $\mathcal P_j(v)=M_j^{-1}v$ for an invertible $M_j$
([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]]).
Equip each coordinate space $\mathbb C^q$ used below with the standard
Hermitian inner product
$$\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_{a<q}z_a\overline{w_a}$$
and its induced Euclidean norm $\|z\|_2=\sqrt{\langle z,z\rangle}$
([[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]], [[def-inner-product-norm]]).
All arithmetic and orthogonalization are exact. Iteration and auxiliary
Hessenberg labels below start at $1$; coordinates of $A$ and ambient vectors
retain the library's zero-based convention.

The algorithm uses and stores each actual $z_j$ and makes no fixed-matrix
assumption.

Set $r_0=b-Ax_0$ and $\beta=\|r_0\|_2$. If $\beta=0$, return
`initial-solution($x_0$)`. Otherwise set $v_1=r_0/\beta$. For
$j=1,\ldots,m$, perform:

1. Obtain $z_j=\mathcal P_j(v_j)$ and set $w:=Az_j$.
2. For $i=1,\ldots,j$ in order, set
   $$h_{ij}:=\langle w,v_i\rangle,\qquad w:=w-h_{ij}v_i.$$
3. Set $h_{j+1,j}:=\|w\|_2$. If $h_{j+1,j}=0$, return
   `breakdown($j,x_{j-1}$)` with the last fully formed iterate (for $j=1$ it
   is $x_0$); do not normalize or claim a new iterate at this step.
4. If $h_{j+1,j}>0$, set $v_{j+1}:=w/h_{j+1,j}$. Let $e_0\in\mathbb C^{j+1}$
   be the standard unit vector at coordinate $0$ (coordinate $0$ is $1$ and
   all other coordinates are $0$; [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The
   iteration labels $h_{ik}$ remain one-based, while matrix slots are
   zero-based: put $Z_j\in M_{n\times j}(\mathbb C)$ with
   $(Z_j)_{a,k-1}=(z_k)_a$ for $0\le a<n$, $1\le k\le j$, and let
   $\bar H_j\in M_{(j+1)\times j}(\mathbb C)$ satisfy
   $(\bar H_j)_{i-1,k-1}=h_{ik}$ for $1\le k\le j$, $1\le i\le k+1$, and
   $(\bar H_j)_{a,b}=0$ when $a>b+1$. Choose any
   $$y_j\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb C^j}\|\beta e_0-\bar H_jy\|_2$$
   and set $x_j:=x_0+Z_jy_j$.

If all $m$ steps complete without breakdown, return
`budget-complete($m,x_m,Z_m$)`. The finite-dimensional least-squares minimizer
exists because each coordinate space $\mathbb C^q$ is finite-dimensional by
[[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]], and the least-squares theorem
[[thm-least-squares-solutions-and-normal-equation]] applies; the output
relation permits any minimizer. The algorithm has no
convergence test: `budget-complete` and `breakdown` assert neither convergence
nor that a breakdown iterate solves $Ax=b$. The residual-minimization property
over the actual span of the $z_j$ is proved separately in
[[thm-flexible-gmres-residual-minimization-on-actual-preconditioned-span]].
Every division is by a positive real norm: the initial $\beta=0$ case returns
before normalizing $r_0$, and each later $h_{j+1,j}=0$ case returns before
normalizing $w$.

## Statement

Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ and $b,x_0\in\mathbb C^n$, with the standard
Hermitian inner product and induced Euclidean norm. Suppose the algorithm
[[alg-flexible-gmres-variable-right-preconditioning]] completes $m\ge1$ steps
without breakdown, producing $Z_m=[z_1,\ldots,z_m]$ and $\bar H_m$. Define
$\beta=\|b-Ax_0\|_2$, let $e_0\in\mathbb C^{m+1}$ be the standard unit
vector at coordinate $0$, and define $V_{m+1}\in M_{n\times(m+1)}(\mathbb C)$
by $(V_{m+1})_{a,i-1}=(v_i)_a$ for $0\le a<n$, $1\le i\le m+1$. The
one-based column label $i$ therefore occupies zero-based matrix column $i-1$.
The matrices $Z_m$ and $\bar H_m$ use the algorithm's one-based-to-zero-based
slot mapping. Then
$$AZ_m=V_{m+1}\bar H_m,$$
and every $y\in\mathbb C^m$ satisfies
$$b-A(x_0+Z_my)=V_{m+1}(\beta e_0-\bar H_my),\qquad \|b-A(x_0+Z_my)\|_2=\|\beta e_0-\bar H_my\|_2.$$
Consequently every least-squares minimizer $y_m$ in the algorithm produces a
true-residual minimizer $x_m=x_0+Z_my_m$ over
$$x_0+\operatorname{span}\{z_1,\ldots,z_m\}.$$
Moreover, $\bar H_m$ has full column rank, so its least-squares minimizer is
unique.
The result makes no fixed-preconditioner spectral or convergence claim.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A system $Ax=b$, an initial vector $x_0$, and a completed $m$-step
run of the variable-right-preconditioned flexible GMRES algorithm with no
breakdown.

[F1] [[alg-flexible-gmres-variable-right-preconditioning]]: the initialization
sets $r_0=b-Ax_0$, $\beta=\|r_0\|_2$, and, when $\beta\ne0$,
$v_1=r_0/\beta$.

[F2] [[alg-flexible-gmres-variable-right-preconditioning]]: each column starts
with $w=Az_j$; the ordered updates use $h_{ij}=\langle w,v_i\rangle$ and
$w:=w-h_{ij}v_i$; after them $h_{j+1,j}=\|w\|_2$, and a positive value
normalizes $v_{j+1}=w/h_{j+1,j}$.

[F3] [[alg-flexible-gmres-variable-right-preconditioning]]: in zero-based
matrix coordinates, $(\bar H_j)_{i-1,k-1}=h_{ik}$ for
$1\le k\le j$, $1\le i\le k+1$, and $(\bar H_j)_{a,b}=0$ when $a>b+1$;
the algorithm minimizes $\|\beta e_0-\bar H_jy\|_2$.

[F4] [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]: on each $\mathbb C^q$,

in its first argument.

[F5] [[def-inner-product-norm]]: the induced norm is
$\|v\|_2=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$.

[F6] [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]: matrix multiplication is
defined by the finite coordinate sums, so its columns act linearly on vectors.

[F7] [[thm-least-squares-solutions-and-normal-equation]]: a linear map between
finite-dimensional inner-product spaces has a least-squares minimizer, and any
two minimizers differ by an element of the map's kernel.

[F8] [[def-linear-combination-and-span]]: $\operatorname{span}(S)$ is the
smallest linear subspace containing $S$.

[F9] [[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]]: a vector belongs to

elements of $S$.

[F10] [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]: $\mathbb C$ is a field, so the
finite coordinate spaces and matrices in the statement are over a field.

[F11] [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]: for every $q\in\mathbb N$, $\mathbb C^q$

finite-dimensional; in particular its standard unit vector at coordinate $0$

At the $i$th Gram–Schmidt substep, the current vector $w$ is orthogonal to $v_k$ for $k<i$. The update $w':=w-h_{ij}v_i$, with $h_{ij}=\langle w,v_i\rangle$, satisfies $\langle w',v_i\rangle=h_{ij}-h_{ij}\langle v_i,v_i\rangle=0$ and $\langle w',v_k\rangle=\langle w,v_k\rangle-h_{ij}\langle v_i,v_k\rangle=0$ for each $k<i$.
