## Statement refuted

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice, which are the hypotheses used by the reduced-gradient supplier.

The pointwise control-only condition from [[thm-ctrl1-lqr-variational-inequality-and-pointwise-control-branch]] holds for an LQR minimizer even when the feasible set includes arbitrary terminal constraints.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Take $T=1$, scalar state and control, $x(0)=0$, dynamics $\dot x=u$, control set $U_c=[0,2]$, and terminal constraint $x(1)=0$. Let $Q=R=1$, $x_d(t)=1$, $P=0$, and $x_T=0$, so $\mathcal F=\{u\in L^2(0,1):0\le u(t)\le2\text{ a.e.},\int_0^1u(t)dt=0\}$. Use the adjoint and derivative conventions of [[def-ctrl1-lqr-adjoint-equation]] and [[lem-ctrl1-lqr-adjoint-identity-and-gradient]].

[A1] Countable Choice and Dependent Choice are assumed for the reduced-gradient supplier ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]).

[F1] A nonnegative function with integral zero vanishes almost everywhere ([[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]]).

[F2] The adjoint satisfies $-\dot p=x-x_d$ and $p(1)=P(x(1)-x_T)$; the reduced gradient is $p+u$ ([[def-ctrl1-lqr-adjoint-equation]], [[lem-ctrl1-lqr-adjoint-identity-and-gradient]]).

## Counterexample

The feasible set in the Given data is determined exactly by the zero terminal-state constraint.

1.1 For every feasible $u$, [F1] applied to $u\ge0$ and $\int_0^1u=0$ gives $u=0$ almost everywhere. Thus $\mathcal F=\{0\}$ and $u^*=0$ is its unique feasible control and hence a minimizer. [F1, given]

## Definition

For each integer $n\ge0$, define the Legendre polynomial
$$
P_n(x):=\frac{1}{2^n n!}\frac{d^n}{dx^n}(x^2-1)^n,
$$
with $n!$ as in [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]] and repeated derivatives as in [[def-higher-derivatives-and-smoothness]]. Define the unweighted pairing of real polynomials by
$$
\langle p,q\rangle_L:=\int_{-1}^1p(x)q(x)\,dx,\qquad \|p\|_L^2:=\langle p,p\rangle_L.
$$
The integral is the ordinary integral of a continuous function. The normalization and all polynomial identities needed for the orthogonal Galerkin scale are proved in [[lem-legendre-weighted-derivative-orthogonality-and-norm]].

## Statement

For $m,n\ge0$, the polynomials of [[def-legendre-polynomial-family-and-l2-pairing]] satisfy
$$
\int_{-1}^1P_n(x)P_m(x)\,dx=\frac{2}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn},
\qquad
\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'(x)P_m'(x)\,dx=\frac{2n(n+1)}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn},
$$
where $\delta_{mn}=1$ if $m=n$ and $0$ otherwise. Each $P_n$ has degree $n$ and nonzero leading coefficient, so $P_0,\ldots,P_N$ form a basis of polynomials of degree at most $N$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Nonnegative integers $m,n$ and the Rodrigues polynomials $P_k$.

[F1] [[def-legendre-polynomial-family-and-l2-pairing]]: $P_n=(2^nn!)^{-1}D^n(x^2-1)^n$ and $\langle p,q\rangle_L=\int_{-1}^1pq$.

[F2] [[thm-integration-by-parts]]: for differentiable factors with integrable derivatives on a closed interval, $\int uv'=[uv]-\int u'v$.

[F3] [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]]: $D(x^k)=kx^{k-1}$ for positive integer $k$, and constants differentiate to zero; repeated application gives the derivatives of monomials.

[F4] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: polynomial sums, products, and scalar multiples obey the usual derivative rules.

## Proof

1.1 Write $(x^2-1)^n=(x-1)^n(x+1)^n$. For every $j<n$, its $j$th derivative vanishes at both endpoints: by the product rule, every term differentiates each factor at most $j<n$ times and retains a positive power of the factor that vanishes at that endpoint. Thus $n$ integrations by parts in [F2] give, for every polynomial $q$ of degree less than $n$, $\int_{-1}^1P_nq=\frac{(-1)^n}{2^nn!}\int_{-1}^1(x^2-1)^nq^{(n)}=0,$ because $q^{(n)}=0$ by [F3]. Hence $P_n$ is orthogonal to every lower-degree polynomial. [F1, F2, F3, F4, given, induction]

2.1 The leading term of $(x^2-1)^n$ is $x^{2n}$; differentiating it $n$ times gives $(2n)!/n!$ times $x^n$ by [F3]. All other terms have lower degree after differentiation. Therefore $P_n$ has degree $n$ and leading coefficient $\kappa_n=(2n)!/(2^n(n!)^2)>0$. The distinct degrees imply the family $P_0,\ldots,P_N$ is linearly independent and spans every polynomial of degree at most $N$, by successive elimination of leading terms. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Since $P_n-\kappa_nx^n$ has degree less than $n$, step 1.1 gives $\int_{-1}^1P_n^2=\kappa_n\int_{-1}^1P_nx^n.$ Apply [F2] $n$ times to the Rodrigues formula against $x^n$. The endpoint terms vanish as in step 1.1 and $(x^n)^{(n)}=n!$, so $\int_{-1}^1P_nx^n=\frac1{2^n}\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)^n\,dx.$ [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Put $J_n=\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)^n dx$. Then $J_0=2$. For $n\ge1$, the endpoint values of $x(1-x^2)^n$ are zero, so integrating its derivative gives $0=J_n-2n(J_{n-1}-J_n),\qquad J_n=\frac{2n}{2n+1}J_{n-1}.$ Induction yields $J_n=2^{2n+1}(n!)^2/(2n+1)!$. Substituting this and $\kappa_n$ from step 2.1 into step 3.1 gives $\int P_n^2=2/(2n+1)$. Together with step 1.1 this proves the first orthogonality formula, including $n=0$. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, induction, algebra]

5.1 When $n=0$, $P_0=1$ and $Q_0=-((1-x^2)P_0')'=0$, so $Q_0=0\cdot P_0$. Now take $n\ge1$ and define $Q_n=-((1-x^2)P_n')'$. Its leading term is $n(n+1)\kappa_nx^n$, so $Q_n-n(n+1)P_n$ has degree less than $n$. For any polynomial $q$ of degree less than $n$, two integrations by parts give $\int_{-1}^1Q_nq=\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'q'=-\int_{-1}^1P_n((1-x^2)q')'=0,$ where both boundary terms vanish because of the factor $1-x^2$, and the last polynomial paired with $P_n$ has degree less than $n$, so step 1.1 applies. Therefore $Q_n-n(n+1)P_n$ is a lower-degree polynomial orthogonal to every lower-degree polynomial. Expand it in the basis from step 2.1; the first formula and the positive norms in step 4.1 force every coefficient to be zero. Thus $Q_n=n(n+1)P_n$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 One integration by parts and step 5.1 give $\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'P_m'=\int_{-1}^1Q_nP_m=n(n+1)\int_{-1}^1P_nP_m.$ The first formula, already proved in step 4.1 and step 1.1, yields the displayed weighted derivative identity for every $m,n\ge0$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

For a relation $A\subseteq E\times E$ and $\rho>0$, define its resolvent as
the inverse relation
$$J_{\rho A}:=(I+\rho A)^{-1},\qquad J_{\rho A}(y)=\{x\in E:y-x\in\rho A(x)\},$$
where $\rho A(x)=\{\rho a:a\in A(x)\}$. Its domain is the set of $y$ for
which this value set is nonempty. At this point it may be partial and
set-valued; full domain and single-valuedness are separate conclusions of
[[thm-maximal-monotone-resolvent-is-firmly-nonexpansive]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A relation $A$ on $E$ and a scalar $\rho>0$.

[A1] The relation is on $E$ and $\rho>0$.


[F1] [[def-maximal-monotone-relation-on-euclidean-space]]: $A(x)$ denotes the set of $a$ with $(x,a)\in A$.

## Proof


1.1 The equation $y-x\in\rho A(x)$ means that some $a\in A(x)$ satisfies $y=x+\rho a$; this is precisely the inverse graph of $I+\rho A$. [A1, given, F1, given]

2.1 The value $J_{\rho A}(y)$ is a set and may be empty until a theorem proves existence; the definition itself asserts no surjectivity or uniqueness. [A1, given, F1, given] ∎

## Statement

Let $A$ be maximal monotone on $E=\mathbb R^n$ and let $\rho>0$. For every
$y\in E$ there is a unique $x\in E$ with $y-x\in\rho A(x)$. Thus the
resolvent from [[def-resolvent-of-a-monotone-relation]] is an everywhere-defined
map and, for all $y,y'\in E$,
$$\|J_{\rho A}y-J_{\rho A}y'\|_2^2\le \langle J_{\rho A}y-J_{\rho A}y',y-y'\rangle.$$
This is firm nonexpansiveness; it also implies the map is 1-Lipschitz.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A maximal-monotone relation $A$ and $\rho>0$.

[A1] The relation $A$ is maximal monotone and $\rho>0$.


[F1] [[def-maximal-monotone-relation-on-euclidean-space]]: monotonicity means $\langle x-x',a-a'\rangle\ge0$ for graph pairs, and maximality excludes any proper monotone graph extension.

[F2] [[def-resolvent-of-a-monotone-relation]]: $x\in J_{\rho A}(y)$ iff $y=x+\rho a$ for some $a\in A(x)$.

[F3] [[lem-one-point-extension-for-finite-dimensional-nonexpansive-map]]: a 1-Lipschitz map on any subset of $E$ admits a value at each added point satisfying all 1-Lipschitz inequalities.

[F4] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: $|\langle v,w\rangle|\le\|v\|_2\|w\|_2$.

## Proof


1.1 Transform every graph pair $(x,a)\in A$ into $p=x+\rho a$ and $q=x-\rho a$. If two graph pairs are used, then $$\|q-q'\|_2^2\le\|p-p'\|_2^2,$$ because the difference of the right and left sides is $4\rho\langle x-x',a-a'\rangle\ge0$ by [F1]. Also, if $p=p'$, this inequality forces $q=q'$. Thus the rule $T(p)=q$ is a well-defined 1-Lipschitz map on its range $D=\{x+\rho a:(x,a)\in A\}$. [A1, F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 Fix arbitrary $y\in E$. By [F3], extend $T$ at $y$ by some $q$ satisfying $\|q-(x-\rho a)\|_2\le\|y-(x+\rho a)\|_2$ for every $(x,a)\in A$. Set $\tilde x=(y+q)/2$ and $\tilde a=(y-q)/(2\rho)$. Expanding the squared inequality shows $\langle\tilde x-x,\tilde a-a\rangle\ge0$ for every graph pair, so adjoining $(\tilde x,\tilde a)$ preserves monotonicity. By maximality in [F1], it already belongs to $A$. Hence $y=\tilde x+\rho\tilde a$, proving existence. This also covers an initially empty graph: [F3] gives the extension and maximality rules out the empty graph. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $x,x'$ both satisfy $y-x\in\rho A(x)$ and $y-x'\in\rho A(x')$, monotonicity gives $0\le\langle x-x',(y-x)-(y-x')\rangle=-\|x-x'\|_2^2$. Thus $x=x'$, so the resolvent is single-valued. [A1, F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For inputs $y,y'$, write $x=J_{\rho A}y$, $x'=J_{\rho A}y'$. Monotonicity applied to $(x,(y-x)/\rho)$ and $(x',(y'-x')/\rho)$ gives $$\|x-x'\|_2^2\le\langle x-x',y-y'\rangle.$$ Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] then gives $\|x-x'\|_2\le\|y-y'\|_2$ when $x\ne x'$, and the inequality is immediate when $x=x'$. This proves firm nonexpansiveness and the Lipschitz consequence. [A1, F1, F2, F4, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Fix $a>0$, put $E=[a,\infty)$, and define the weight $w(x)=1+x^2$. Let $\mathcal M_w(E)$ be the real vector space of finite signed Borel measures $\sigma$ on $E$ for which

$$\|\sigma\|_w:=\int_E w(x)\,|\sigma|(dx)<\infty,$$

where $|\sigma|$ is the total-variation measure. The norm is $\|\cdot\|_w$. A positive population measure is a nonnegative member $\mu\in\mathcal M_w(E)$. Its number, mass, and second moment are $M_0(\mu)=\int_E1\,d\mu$, $M_1(\mu)=\int_Ex\,d\mu$, and $M_2(\mu)=\int_Ex^2\,d\mu$. The space and its completeness are established in [[lem-weighted-total-variation-space-is-complete]].

## Statement

The normed vector space $\mathcal M_w(E)$ of [[def-weighted-total-variation-space-for-population-measures]] is complete.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $E=[a,\infty)$, $w(x)=1+x^2$, and $\mathcal M_w(E)$ with norm $\|\sigma\|_w=\int w\,d|\sigma|$.

[F1] [[def-weighted-total-variation-space-for-population-measures]]: $\mathcal M_w(E)$ consists of finite signed Borel measures with $\int w\,d|\sigma|<\infty$, and $\|\sigma\|_w=\int w\,d|\sigma|$.

## Proof

1.1 The map $J:\sigma\mapsto w\sigma$ is linear. Multiplication by the positive function $w$ gives $|w\sigma|=w|\sigma|$, so [F1] yields $\|J\sigma\|_{TV}=\|\sigma\|_w$. It is onto because for any finite signed measure $\eta$, $\sigma=w^{-1}\eta$ satisfies $J\sigma=\eta$ and $\|\sigma\|_w=\int w\,d|w^{-1}\eta|=\|\eta\|_{TV}$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 Let $(\eta_n)$ be Cauchy in total variation. Choose increasing indices $n_j$ with $\|\eta_{n_{j+1}}-\eta_{n_j}\|_{TV}\le2^{-j}$, taking the least qualifying index at each step. For each Borel set $A$, the series $\eta_{n_1}(A)+\sum_{j\ge1}(\eta_{n_{j+1}}-\eta_{n_j})(A)$ converges absolutely, uniformly in $A$, because each summand is bounded by its total-variation norm. Define $\eta(A)$ by that sum. If $(A_k)$ are disjoint, the double series of absolute values is bounded by $\|\eta_{n_1}\|_{TV}+\sum_j\|\eta_{n_{j+1}}-\eta_{n_j}\|_{TV}$, so the two countable sums may be interchanged; hence $\eta$ is countably additive. The same tail bound gives $\|\eta-\eta_{n_j}\|_{TV}\le\sum_{r\ge j}2^{-r}\to0$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $j$ so this is below $\varepsilon/2$ and the Cauchy property gives $\|\eta_n-\eta_m\|_{TV}<\varepsilon/2$ for all $n,m\ge n_j$. For any $n\ge n_j$, choose $n_k\ge n_j$ and pass to the limit in $\|\eta_n-\eta_{n_k}\|_{TV}<\varepsilon/2$; since $\eta_{n_k}\to\eta$, this gives $\|\eta_n-\eta\|_{TV}\le\varepsilon/2<\varepsilon$. Thus finite signed measures are complete in total variation. [given, choose]

2.1 Pulling the limit $\eta$ back through the inverse isometry $w^{-1}$ gives a limit in $\mathcal M_w(E)$ for every Cauchy sequence there. [step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Example

Take the complex finite-basis PC-VAR energy $E(P)$ and Hermitian gradient
$F(P)$ from [[def-finite-basis-projector-energy-model]] and
[[prop-finite-projector-energy-reality-and-gradient]]. The model's domain is
the rank-$r$ Hermitian projector set, with $1\le r<n$. A complex orthonormal
frame $X\in\operatorname{St}_{\mathbb C}(n,r)$ represents $P=XX^*$, and
unitary frame changes preserve $P$. The model-specific Grassmann gradient is
$$\operatorname{grad}E([X])=2(I-P)F(P)X.$$

Start from any $X_0\in\operatorname{St}_{\mathbb C}(n,r)$ and set
$x_0=[X_0]$. Choose $0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1$,
$0<\gamma_{\rm dec}<1<\gamma_{\rm inc}$, $0<\theta_C\le1$,
$\Delta_{\max}>0$, $0<\Delta_0\le\Delta_{\max}$, and
$0<\varepsilon\le1$; use an outer cap at least the bound in
[[thm-riemannian-trust-region-first-order-complexity]].

Use the complex polar retraction and the finite-budget trust-region method of
[[alg-riemannian-trust-region]], with the inner subproblem routine returning
failure immediately so the method uses its explicit Cauchy fallback. Since

positive radius. The polar map preserves the projector's Hermitian, idempotent,
rank-$r$ constraints at every trial; rejected trials
leave the current projector unchanged. Because the finite-basis energy is
$C^2$ on a neighborhood and the complex Grassmannian is compact, its pullback
gradients are uniformly Lipschitz on every fixed bounded tangent disk. Choose
the zero self-adjoint model operator, which is uniformly bounded. Thus the
hypotheses of [[thm-riemannian-trust-region-first-order-complexity]] hold, and
its first-order target is reached within the theorem's explicit
$O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ accepted and rejected outer-trial bound when the finite
cap is chosen accordingly. This is a finite-dimensional optimization
guarantee; no claim is made that an arbitrary selected exchange-correlation
functional models exact continuum physics.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite-basis PC-VAR model of [[def-finite-basis-projector-energy-model]], its real-valued $C^2$ energy and Hermitian Frobenius gradient ([[prop-finite-projector-energy-reality-and-gradient]]), $1\le r<n$, and an initial frame $X_0\in\operatorname{St}_{\mathbb C}(n,r)$ defining $x_0=[X_0]$.

[F1] The model defines $E(P)=\operatorname{tr}(hP)+\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(PG(P))+E_{xc}(P)$ on rank-$r$ Hermitian projectors ([[def-finite-basis-projector-energy-model]]).

[F2] The real-valued $C^2$ energy has Hermitian Frobenius gradient $F(P)$ ([[prop-finite-projector-energy-reality-and-gradient]]).

[F3] The complex Grassmann tangent is represented by $X^*Z=0$ and projects by $(I-XX^*)G$ ([[thm-complex-stiefel-grassmann-tangent-projections]]).

[F4] The gradient of a Hermitian projector energy with gradient $K(P)$ is $2(I-XX^*)K(P)X$ ([[prop-complex-grassmann-projector-energy-gradient]]).

[F5] Complex Grassmann is compact, and its polar map is defined on horizontal vectors, maps to orthonormal frames, is smooth, and has frame differential $D R_X^{\rm pol}(0)[\eta]=\eta$ ([[prop-complex-stiefel-grassmann-are-compact]], [[def-complex-grassmann-polar-retraction]], [[thm-complex-grassmann-polar-retraction-is-first-order]]).

[F6] The trust-region method uses a retracted trial, leaves the current point on rejection, and has the proved first-order count under its pullback hypotheses ([[alg-riemannian-trust-region]], [[thm-riemannian-trust-region-first-order-complexity]]).

[F7] Every finite-dimensional complex inner-product subspace has an orthonormal basis ([[cor-finite-dimensional-inner-product-spaces-have-orthonormal-bases]]).

[F8] Closed bounded subsets of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space are compact ([[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]]).

[F9] A continuous real-valued function on a compact metric space attains its maximum ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** identify the PC-VAR projector domain with the unitary quotient, compute its gradient, and verify trust-region regularity.

1.1 If $X^*X=I_r$, then $P=XX^*$ is Hermitian and $P^2=X(X^*X)X^*=P$, with range equal to the column space of $X$ and therefore rank $r$. For unitary $Q$, $(XQ)(XQ)^*=XQQ^*X^*=P$. Thus $E(XX^*)$ is unitary-invariant and descends to complex Grassmann by [F1]. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 For every horizontal $Z$, [F2] and [F4] yield the complex Grassmann gradient $2(I-P)F(P)X$. This formula uses the real derivative of the Hermitian-matrix energy, as required for a real-valued objective on complex coordinates. [F2, F3, F4, given, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Conversely, let $P$ be any rank-$r$ orthogonal projector. Choose an orthonormal basis of its $r$-dimensional range by [F7] and collect its vectors as the columns of $X$. Then $X^*X=I_r$ and $XX^*=P$, so the parameterization covers exactly the model's projector domain. By [F5], the polar-retracted trial remains a complex orthonormal frame, so its projector remains Hermitian, idempotent, and rank $r$; rejection leaves the old projector unchanged by [F6]. [F5, F6, F7, given, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Fix any finite $\Delta_{\max}>0$. The set of pairs $(X,\eta)$ with $X^*X=I_r$, $X^*\eta=0$, and $\|\eta\|_F\le\Delta_{\max}$ is closed and bounded in a finite-dimensional real coordinate space, hence compact by [F8]. The polar retraction is smooth on it, and [F1]–[F2] make the pullback energy $C^2$ along the horizontal tangent bundle. Its fiber Hessian is continuous on this compact set, so its operator norm has a finite maximum by [F9]. Integrating this Hessian along each fiber segment gives a uniform Lipschitz bound for the pullback gradient. Choose the model operator $B_x=0$, which is self-adjoint and uniformly bounded by $M_B=0$. Hence all regularity and model hypotheses in [F6] hold, and a finite cap at least the theorem's trial bound suffices. [F1, F2, F5, F6, F8, F9, given, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $S=S^*\succ0$ be an $n\times n$ finite-basis overlap matrix and supply its
Cholesky factor $L$ with $S=LL^*$, $L$ invertible
([[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]],
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]).
If $h_0=h_0^*$ is the coefficient-basis one-body matrix, set
$h=L^{-1}h_0L^{-*}$, where $L^{-*}=(L^*)^{-1}$; this is the Cholesky
whitening whose generalized Ritz quotient is preserved by
[[prop-positive-definite-overlap-whitening-preserves-generalized-ritz-pencil]].
For coefficient vectors use $y=L^*c$; the interaction map and chosen
exchange-correlation functional below are supplied in these orthonormal
coordinates. Fix $1\le r<n$ and the
projector domain $\mathcal P_r$ of [[def-rank-r-orthogonal-projector-domain]].

Supply a Hermitian matrix $h$, a real-linear self-adjoint map
$G:\mathbb H_n\to\mathbb H_n$ for the Frobenius inner product, and a real-valued
$C^2$ functional $E_{xc}$ on an open neighborhood of $\mathcal P_r$. Define
$$E(P):=\operatorname{tr}(hP)+\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(P G(P))+E_{xc}(P),\qquad F(P):=h+G(P)+\nabla E_{xc}(P).$$
Here $F(P)$ is the Hermitian Frobenius-gradient formula justified by
[[prop-finite-projector-energy-reality-and-gradient]].

The finite-basis Hartree–Fock model is the special case $E_{xc}=0$ with a
supplied symmetry-compatible Coulomb/exchange tensor defining $G$. A
Kohn–Sham-like model supplies its density map and chosen differentiable
exchange-correlation functional. These are finite-dimensional mathematical
models; this definition makes no assertion that the selected functional is an
exact continuum physical energy.

## Statement

For the data of [[def-finite-basis-projector-energy-model]], $E(P)$ is real
and $C^2$ on its stated neighborhood. For every Hermitian $P$ in that
neighborhood and every Hermitian direction $H$,
$$DE(P)[H]=\operatorname{tr}\big((h+G(P)+\nabla E_{xc}(P))H\big)=\langle F(P),H\rangle_F.$$
Thus $F(P)$ is the Hermitian Frobenius gradient of $E$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Hermitian $h,P,H$, a real-linear self-adjoint map $G$ on $\mathbb H_n$, and a real $C^2$ functional $E_{xc}$ on an open neighborhood of $P$.

[F1] Trace and Frobenius-linear functionals differentiate by their linear increments ([[prop-differentials-of-trace-and-frobenius-linear-functionals]]).

[F2] Matrix differentials obey the sum, product, and adjoint rules ([[prop-matrix-differentials-obey-sum-product-and-adjoint-rules]]).

[F3] In the projector energy model, $G$ is real-linear and self-adjoint and $E_{xc}$ has its Frobenius gradient ([[def-finite-basis-projector-energy-model]]).

[F4] For conformable matrices over a field, $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$ ([[thm-trace-of-ab-equals-trace-of-ba]]).

## Proof

1.1 If $A,B$ are Hermitian, then $\overline{\operatorname{tr}(AB)}=\operatorname{tr}((AB)^*)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)=\operatorname{tr}(AB)$ by the trace identity [F4]. Hence $\operatorname{tr}(hP)$ and $\operatorname{tr}(P G(P))$ are real; $E_{xc}$ is real by [F3]. The first two terms are polynomial in the real coordinates of $P$, so together with the $C^2$ term they give a real $C^2$ function. [F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]

1.2 For real $t$, real-linearity gives $G(P+tH)=G(P)+tG(H)$. Expanding and collecting the coefficient of $t$ yields $\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}((P+tH)G(P+tH))=\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(H G(P)) +\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(P G(H))$. The linear trace term differentiates to $\operatorname{tr}(hH)$ by [F1], and the $E_{xc}$ term differentiates to $\langle\nabla E_{xc}(P),H\rangle_F$ by its gradient definition. [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Self-adjointness of $G$ gives $\operatorname{tr}(P G(H))=\langle P,G(H)\rangle_F=\langle G(P),H\rangle_F=\operatorname{tr}(G(P)H)$. Since these traces are real, the two quadratic contributions in step 1.2 combine to $\operatorname{tr}(G(P)H)$. Adding the other derivatives gives $DE(P)[H]=\langle h+G(P)+\nabla E_{xc}(P),H\rangle_F$. This is the unique Frobenius gradient pairing, so it equals $\langle F(P),H\rangle_F$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎
